Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory.﴾ ﴿That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what will follow, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And that Allah may aid you with a mighty victory.﴾

The opening of the speech with the particle (inna) arises from the sorrow that had afflicted the Muslims, because the polytheists were answered in their request for a truce, as will come in the report of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and as preceded in the report of 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. Thus the emphasis is directed at the listeners by way of indirect allusion (ta'rid). As for the Prophet ﷺ, he was certain of this, and the explanation of this emphasis will come shortly.

Al-fath (opening/victory): the removal of the lock of a door or a storehouse. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ [al-A'raf: 40]. It is also applied to victory, and to the entry of a warrior into the lands of his enemy, because the land and territory of every people is defended. So the warrior's forcing his way into it after battle resembles the removal of the lock from a house or a storehouse. For this reason, the use of "fath" for victory accompanied by entry into the land or city of the defeated became common, and it was not applied to a victory whose outcome was booty and captives without entering the land. Hence one says "the Conquest of Khaybar" and "the Conquest of Makkah," but one does not say "the Conquest of Badr" or "the Conquest of Uhud." Whoever applies "fath" to victory in general has been lax. How could he, when victory has been conjoined with opening in His saying: ﴿Victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾ [al-Saff: 13], in surah al-Saff?

Perhaps what led them to count victory among the meanings of the root f-t-h is that the conquest of lands is the greatest victory, since victory is realized through overpowering and through booty. When it occurs together with entering the enemy's land, that is a great victory, because it is not complete except with the enemy's utterly shameful defeat and his incapacity to defend his land.

"Fath" has also been applied to judgment (hukm), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "When is this judgment, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 28], the verse of surah al-Sajdah.

Out of regard for this meaning, a group of exegetes said: the intended meaning of "fath" here is the Conquest of Makkah, and its interpretation is as a promise of conquest, meaning: "We will open." The reports speak in the past tense only to affirm its certainty and assurance; the future time is treated as if it were past, so the form used for the past is employed for it.

Or we may say that "fathna" is used with the meaning "We have decreed for you the conquest," and this usage is one of the Qur'an's own technical expressions, because it is speech from one who has disposal over things, whom no obstacle prevents from disposing of them. It also follows the custom of Allah's reports, because there is no doubt in His report, and this is further a metonymy (kinayah) for the exaltation of the one who reports, like ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

Among what falls under this interpretation is that the intended meaning of "fath" is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, likening it to the Conquest of Makkah, because it was a preparation for it. Thus it is reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "We did not count the Conquest of Makkah except as the day of al-Hudaybiyah," meaning that they were certain of the occurrence of the Conquest of Makkah through this promise. And it is reported from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: "You count the conquest to be the Conquest of Makkah, and indeed the Conquest of Makkah was a conquest. Yet many indications favor that the intended meaning of "fath" in surah al-Fath is something else. The first is that He described it as "clear" (mubin).

The third: His saying ﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 18].

For this reason the agent is not made explicit in ﴿and complete His favor upon you and guide you﴾, because His bestowing of favor upon him is known, and his guidance is known; He only informed about an increase in these two.

And the completion of the blessing: giving him what He had not given him of the kinds of blessing, such as the Islam of the Quraysh and the liberation of all the land of the Hijaz so that it entered under his rule, and the submission of those who opposed him and fought him. This looks to His saying - exalted is He - ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My blessing upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. That is what the Messenger ﷺ was promised in this verse, and it was realized after years.

The meaning of ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾: He increases you in guidance that had not been preceded, by widening the explanation of the Shari'ah and by making known what had not previously been made known to him of it. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory.﴾ ﴿That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what will follow, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And that Allah may aid you with a mighty victory.﴾

The opening of the speech with the particle (inna) arises from the sorrow that had afflicted the Muslims, because the polytheists were answered in their request for a truce, as will come in the report of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and as preceded in the report of 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal. Thus the emphasis is directed at the listeners by way of indirect allusion (ta'rid). As for the Prophet ﷺ, he was certain of this, and the explanation of this emphasis will come shortly.

Al-fath (opening/victory): the removal of the lock of a door or a storehouse. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ [al-A'raf: 40]. It is also applied to victory, and to the entry of a warrior into the lands of his enemy, because the land and territory of every people is defended. So the warrior's forcing his way into it after battle resembles the removal of the lock from a house or a storehouse. For this reason, the use of "fath" for victory accompanied by entry into the land or city of the defeated became common, and it was not applied to a victory whose outcome was booty and captives without entering the land. Hence one says "the Conquest of Khaybar" and "the Conquest of Makkah," but one does not say "the Conquest of Badr" or "the Conquest of Uhud." Whoever applies "fath" to victory in general has been lax. How could he, when victory has been conjoined with opening in His saying: ﴿Victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾ [al-Saff: 13], in surah al-Saff?

Perhaps what led them to count victory among the meanings of the root f-t-h is that the conquest of lands is the greatest victory, since victory is realized through overpowering and through booty. When it occurs together with entering the enemy's land, that is a great victory, because it is not complete except with the enemy's utterly shameful defeat and his incapacity to defend his land.

[p. 144]

"Fath" has also been applied to judgment (hukm), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "When is this judgment, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 28], the verse of surah al-Sajdah.

Out of regard for this meaning, a group of exegetes said: the intended meaning of "fath" here is the Conquest of Makkah, and its interpretation is as a promise of conquest, meaning: "We will open." The reports speak in the past tense only to affirm its certainty and assurance; the future time is treated as if it were past, so the form used for the past is employed for it.

Or we may say that "fathna" is used with the meaning "We have decreed for you the conquest," and this usage is one of the Qur'an's own technical expressions, because it is speech from one who has disposal over things, whom no obstacle prevents from disposing of them. It also follows the custom of Allah's reports, because there is no doubt in His report, and this is further a metonymy (kinayah) for the exaltation of the one who reports, like ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

Among what falls under this interpretation is that the intended meaning of "fath" is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, likening it to the Conquest of Makkah, because it was a preparation for it. Thus it is reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "We did not count the Conquest of Makkah except as the day of al-Hudaybiyah," meaning that they were certain of the occurrence of the Conquest of Makkah through this promise. And it is reported from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: "You count the conquest to be the Conquest of Makkah, and indeed the Conquest of Makkah was a conquest. But we count the conquest to be the Pledge of Pleasure (bay'at al-Ridwan) on the day of al-Hudaybiyah," meaning that you take "fath" in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory﴾ to refer to the conquest of the Pledge of Pleasure, although the name "fath" is mostly applied to the Conquest of Makkah.

This interpretation is supported by the report of 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal: "The Messenger of Allah recited surah al-Fath on the day of the Conquest of Makkah," and in another narration: "He entered Makkah while reciting surah al-Fath on his riding beast."

Yet many indications favor that the intended meaning of "fath" in surah al-Fath is something else. The first is that He described it as "clear" (mubin).

The second: that He made its cause "the mighty victory," and a thing is not the cause of itself.

[p. 145]

The third: His saying ﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 18].

The fourth: His saying ﴿And much booty that you will take﴾ [al-Fath: 19].

The fifth: His saying ﴿So He made, besides that, a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

The majority hold that the intended meaning in surah al-Fath is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. They regarded applying the name "fath" to it as a metonymy by a sending relation (majaz mursal), in view of its consequence leading to the Conquest of Khaybar and the Conquest of Makkah, or its being a cause of them. Thus it is reported from al-Zuhri: "The Day of al-Hudaybiyah was truly the greatest of the conquests, for the Prophet ﷺ came to it with fourteen hundred. When the treaty was concluded, people mixed with one another, that is, they dispersed throughout the lands, and some of them entered the lands of others for the sake of security among them. They knew and heard about Allah, and no one wished to embrace Islam without being able to do so. Those two years had not passed before the Muslims had come to Makkah with ten thousand." End of quotation. In another narration: "When the truce took place, people felt secure with one another, met, and engaged in conversation and debate, and no one of intelligence was addressed about Islam without entering it."

On this basis, the metonymy lies in applying the root "fath" to its cause and its outcome, not in the form of the verb. That is, the expression of the future by a past form is not the issue, because by this metonymical consideration it has occurred in the past. Thus the name "fath" is used as a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings, and the past-tense form is used in both of its senses. This clarifies the aspect of inimitability (i'jaz) in choosing this structure.

It was also said that it is the Conquest of Khaybar, which took place on the return from al-Hudaybiyah, as will come in His saying ﴿When you set out toward spoils to take them﴾ [al-Fath: 15].

On these interpretations, the emphasis of the speech with "inna" is due to the hesitation or questioning of some Muslims regarding the occurrence of that. Thus: "It is reported from 'Umar that when ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Is that a conquest, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed a conquest.'" And al-Bayhaqi related from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came back from al-Hudaybiyah, and a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'By Allah, this is not a conquest. We were kept away from the House, and our offering was held back.' This reached the Messenger of Allah, and he said: 'What a wretched word this is! Rather, it is the greatest of conquests. The polytheists have been content that you turn them away from their lands by force, and they ask you for a settlement and seek your safety, though they have disliked from you what they disliked. Allah has granted you victory over them and returned you safe, having gained booty and rewards. This is the greatest conquest. Have you forgotten the Day of Uhud, when you went up and did not turn back for anyone, while I was calling you from behind? Have you forgotten the Day of the Confederates, when ﴿they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]?'" Then the Muslims said: "Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly, and it is indeed the greatest of conquests. By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, we had not reflected on what you have mentioned, and you are more knowledgeable about Allah and about affairs than we are."

The object of "fathna" is omitted, because the intention is to inform about the kind of conquest, not about a specific conquered thing.

The "lam" in His saying "fathna laka" is the lam of cause, meaning: "We have opened for your sake a great conquest," like the one in His saying ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

Placing the prepositional phrase before the absolute object, contrary to the default order of the verb's complements, is for the purpose of stressing and giving attention to this cause.

His saying ﴿That Allah may forgive you﴾ is a comprehensive apposition (badal ishtimal) from the pronoun in "laka." The sense is: "We have opened a clear conquest for your sake, for Allah's forgiveness of you, the completion of His favor upon you, and His guiding you to a straight path, and His aiding you with a mighty victory." Allah's forgiveness of the Prophet ﷺ was made a cause of the conquest because it is among what Allah intended to achieve through the conquest. The particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil) does not require restricting the purpose of the caused act to that single cause, since many things have numerous causes, and some of them are mentioned as suits the context. Since the conquest was for the honor of the Prophet ﷺ with his Lord, the Exalted, it was among its causes that Allah should forgive His Prophet ﷺ a general forgiveness, completing the honor. This is a forgiveness specific to the Prophet ﷺ, different from the forgiveness attained by the fighters through jihad and the conquest.

The meaning, then, is that Allah, when this conquest took place, made the forgiveness of everything for which He might hold His messengers accountable, so that nothing remained for His Messenger ﷺ that would keep him from reaching the utmost limit of excellence among created beings. He made this forgiveness a reward to him for completing his tasks for which he was sent: the conveying, the striving, the toil, and the turning in desire toward Allah.

Since the conquest was achieved through his effort and his causing it, by Allah's facilitation of that for him, Allah made his reward the forgiveness of his sins, in view of the great effect of that conquest: the removal of polytheism, the elevation of the word of Allah, the Exalted, and the perfecting and purifying of souls by faith and righteous deeds, so that goodness spreads with the spread of the religion and righteousness becomes a character trait of people, whereby some follow others. All of this suits only the Conquest of Makkah. This is what the surah of ﴿When the victory of Allah comes﴾ [al-Nasr: 1] contains, in His saying ﴿When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [al-Nasr: 1–3]. That is, at that time you have been forgiven the greatest forgiveness, which is the forgiveness befitting the greatest of those to whom Allah turns in repentance, and it is none other than the forgiveness of all sins, past and whatever may come of them, which the Prophet ﷺ would count as a sin out of intense fear of even the slightest shortcoming. As it is said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near." Although the Prophet ﷺ was protected from committing after that anything for which he would be held accountable.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The intended meaning is the honoring through this ruling, even if he had no sins. And for this subtle and sublime meaning, the surah of ﴿When the victory of Allah comes﴾ was a sign of the approach of the Prophet's ﷺ death, as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas understood, and this has been reported from the Prophet ﷺ."

Taqaddum (preceding) and ta'akhkhur (following) are relative states of existing things, real or conceptual. One says: "The traveler advanced in his journey ahead of the caravan," and one says: "The revelation of such-and-such a surah after such-and-such a surah." Therefore there is frequent need to explain what lay between them in preceding and following, by mentioning the complement of a verb of preceding and following. Sometimes that is omitted, relying on context, and sometimes the relation is disregarded, so that the verb is placed in the position of non-relational verbs, for the sake of generalizing its complements. Most of this occurs when two verbs are combined, as in His saying here: ﴿what preceded of your sin and what will follow﴾.

The intended meaning of "what preceded" is the generalization of forgiveness to sin, like His saying ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. This does not imply that a sin had proceeded from him or that a sin would proceed from him; the purpose is that Allah, the Exalted, raised his rank to the rank of not being held accountable for a sin even if it were supposed to have come from him. The meaning of "sin" was explained earlier, at His saying ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Muhammad: 19], in surah al-Qital.

The verb "liyaghfira" is attributed to the proper name of majesty, Allah, although the apparent expectation would be to attribute it to the concealed pronoun. This was intended to highlight this forgiveness, because the proper noun is more penetrating to the hearing and more effective in drawing attention. This is for the sake of emphasis on the predicate and its complement, since this report is new and the Messenger ﷺ had no knowledge of it. For this reason the agent is not made explicit in ﴿and complete His favor upon you and guide you﴾, because His bestowing of favor upon him is known, and his guidance is known; He only informed about an increase in these two.

﴿It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith along with their faith.﴾

This sentence is a *badal ishtimal* (an apposition of inclusion) relative to the content of the sentence ﴿and Allah helps you with a mighty help﴾ [al-Fath: 3]. From it, the discourse moves to mention the share of the Muslims in this victory. The believers are the soldiers of Allah, through whom the Prophet ﷺ was aided, as He says, ﴿It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62]. Thus, mentioning Allah's care in reforming their souls, removing the whisperings of Satan from them, guiding them to the truth, and firming their resolve and the steadiness of their faith, is a preparation of the causes of the Prophet's ﷺ victory and of the promised conquest, so that they would advance against the enemy, when called to fight, with firm hearts. Do you not see that the believers' souls were thrown into turmoil by the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, when they turned back after it, without entering Mecca, although they had come for the 'umrah with a large number whom they reckoned could not be defeated; and that if the enemy intended them harm or prevented them from their purpose, they would confront it and prevail over it; and that they would enter Mecca by force? They disputed over naming what had befallen them that day a "conquest", as you know from what has preceded. When the Messenger ﷺ explained to them the good that was in it, their souls became calm after agitation, and their certainty became firm after the whisperings of doubt. Had it not been for that tranquillity and firmness, they would have remained distressed in mind and deeply troubled. That tranquillity is what Allah named *sakinah* (tranquillity), and its production in their souls was called "sending down tranquillity into their hearts". Thus the victory included various things, of which the most important is the sending down of tranquillity. The sending down of tranquillity, in relation to this victory, was like the joining together of the hearts of the believers despite the difference of their tribes, and the security that existed between them in the Jahiliyyah, in relation to the victory mentioned in His words, ﴿It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers, and joined their hearts﴾ [al-Anfal: 62].

As for its "sending down" (*inzal*): it is its placement in the intellect and the soul, and the creation of its essential and incidental causes. The act of "sending down" was applied to that placement as an honouring of that inner state, as though it were a thing located on a high place above people, so it was "cast" into people's hearts. This is an imaginative elevation (*rif'ah takhyiliyyah*), intended to express the nobility of what is attributed to it, by way of the imaginative mode.

Since one of the consequences of that tranquillity was that it was a cause for the removal of what Satan cast into their souls by way of interpreting Allah's promise of victory to them other than its apparent meaning, taking it to refer to a spiritual victory, because they deemed it unlikely that this would be a conquest, when Allah sent down tranquillity upon them, their souls became calm, what had crept into them was removed, and they were certain that it was the promise of Allah and that it would come to pass. Thus what was about to cause some of them doubt, and so join the hypocrites who entertain an evil opinion of Allah, was dispelled from them. Indeed, the increase of proofs strengthens the establishment of what is proven in the intellect and the strength of assent.

This is a common usage in the Qur'an. That increase is treated as the cause of the sending down of tranquillity into their hearts, because Allah knew that when tranquillity came into their hearts their faith would be firmly established. Therefore, what is known to occur from the act is treated as the cause, and the particle of causation, the *lam* of *kay*, is applied to it. The strength of faith is treated as another faith added to the earlier faith, because each individual member of a kind, when joined to other individuals, increases their strength. For this reason the adverbial *ma'a* ("along with") is attached to faith in His words, ﴿along with their faith﴾. Thus there was in that event great good for them, just as there was good for the Prophet ﷺ in it, in that it was a cause of honouring him with general forgiveness, of completing the favour upon him, of guiding him to a straight path, and of helping him with a mighty help. How magnificent, then, is the event that brought this good to the Messenger ﷺ and to his companions!

﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement) to the preceding discourse, since it indicates that there is nothing strange in Allah opening for you a great conquest and helping you against many fierce peoples, with a help accompanied by the sending down of tranquillity into the hearts of the believers after failure and broken spirits had crept into them. Allah is the One who possesses all the means of victory, and to Him belongs the overwhelming power in the heavens and the earth. This victory is but a part of the power and dominance that belong to Allah.

The *wa* is *i'tiradiyyah* (parenthetical), and the concluding sentence is a parenthesis between the sentence ﴿that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾ and its dependent clause, which is ﴿that He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens﴾ [al-Fath: 5], and so on.

The term "soldiers" was applied to the causes of victory, by way of likening the causes of victory to the soldiers who fight and prevail.

\[Page 151\]

In placing the concluding sentence after the sentence ﴿It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers﴾, there is an indication that the believers are among the soldiers of Allah, and that the sending down of tranquillity into their hearts is a strengthening of their resolve. Hence, mentioning them specifically before and after this general statement is an honouring of their status. His words later, ﴿that He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens﴾ [al-Fath: 5], and so on, point to this.

Among the soldiers of the heavens are the angels who were sent down on the day of Badr, the wind that was sent against the enemy on the day of the Confederates, and the rain that was sent down on the day of Badr, by which Allah made the feet of the Muslims firm.

Among the soldiers of the earth are the armies of the believers and the numerous tribes who came as believers, fighting alongside the Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, such as the Banu Sulaym, and the delegations of tribes who came as believers, submissive, without fighting, in the Year of Delegations.

*Junud* (soldiers) is the plural of *jund*, and *jund* is a noun for a group of fighters that has no singular from its own form. Its plural is used in consideration of the multiplicity of groups, because an army is composed of soldiers: a vanguard, a right wing, a left wing, a centre, and a rearguard.

The placing of the predicate before the subject in ﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ serves to convey restriction (*hasr*). It is a restriction by claim (*hasr idda'i*), since no account is taken of the soldiers that kings and conquerors gather, given the enemy's dominance, in comparison with the dominance that Allah has over His enemies and the victory He gives to His allies.

The sentence ﴿and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ is a *tadhyil* to what precedes it: the conquest, the victory, and the sending down of tranquillity into the hearts of the believers.

The meaning is that He is Knowing of the causes of the conquest and the victory, and Knowing of what calms the hearts of the believers after their agitation; and He is Wise, placing the requirements of His knowledge in their appropriate places and at their suitable times.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 5:

﴿That He may admit the believing men and the believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally, and remove from them their misdeeds. And that is, with Allah, a great achievement.﴾

The lam here is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and it is connected to the verb in ﴿that they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. So what follows the lam is a cause of the cause of sending down tranquility (al-sakina), and therefore it is also a cause of sending down tranquility, by way of its being a cause of a cause.

Page 152

The mention of the believing women alongside the believing men here serves to ward off the misconception that the promise of this admission is restricted to men. Since the form of the plural is the masculine form, and since this may reinforce that misconception, [the women must be mentioned] because the victory, the triumph, and the soldiers are all, as a cause or a cause of a cause, connected with men. The women have their share in this, however, because they are never free of participation in those hardships, through those of them who tend the sick and the wounded, who give water to the army at the time of fighting, and through the patience of some of them in bereavement or widowhood, and through their patience in the absence of husbands, sons, and close relatives.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿And that was﴾ refers to what was mentioned: Allah's admitting them into the Garden.

The intended sense of their admission into the Garden is a particular admission, namely their admission into the abodes of the fighters (al-mujahidin), and it is not the general admission which they deserve through faith and the other righteous deeds.

For this reason ﴿and remove from them their misdeeds﴾ is conjoined to it.

Al-fawz (triumph) is a verbal noun, meaning the attainment of good and success. The phrase ﴿with Allah﴾ is connected to "fawzan" (a great achievement), meaning that they achieved success with Allah, in the sense that they attained success and triumph in Allah's treatment of them with honor. Placing it before its complement is for the sake of emphasis on this honorable treatment.

The discourse on God's hosts, in the context of mentioning God's victory, necessarily implies a defeated party, namely the enemy, who are overcome by those hosts. Since the victory that God decreed was made conditional on what He announced to the believers, it follows necessarily that it is also conditional on what grieves the enemy and their party. So God mentioned, as the cause of that victory, that through it He punishes the hypocrites, who are the enemy's party, and the polytheists, who are the enemy's core. Accordingly, His words ﴿and He punishes the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women﴾ are coordinated with ﴿that He may admit the believing men and the believing women into gardens﴾ [al-Fath: 5].

The intended meaning is a specific punishment, additional to the punishment they deserved because of their disbelief and hypocrisy. His words after it, ﴿the evil turn of fortune is upon them﴾, hint at this.

[Page 153]

The beginning of the mention of the hypocrites in the punishment, before the polytheists, serves to alert the Muslims that the disbelief of the hypocrites is hidden, so the Muslims may have been heedless of this group or forgotten them.

None of the hypocrites went out to the conquest of Mecca or to the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the make-up 'umrah), because they did not like the polytheists to see them engaged in the deeds of the Muslims and showing solidarity with them. Also, they used to think that the polytheists would repel the Muslims from Mecca and that victory would go to the polytheists.

Punishment ('adhab) means the delivery of torment to them. This is true of worldly punishment by the sword, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God will punish them at your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14], and He said: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. It is also true of fear, of dread of being exposed, and of grief at seeing the believers victorious and safe. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], and He said: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50]. And it is true of the punishment of the Hereafter, which is singled out at the end of the verse by His words ﴿and He has prepared for them Hell﴾.

The coordination of the hypocrite women is like the earlier coordination of the believing women, because the wives of the hypocrites share in their secrets, and they support what the men plot of deception, and they prepare for them the sheltering of the polytheists when they visit them.

His words ﴿the ones who think﴾ (al-zanninin) are an adjective of the mentioned groups: the hypocrite men, the hypocrite women, the polytheist men and the polytheist women. The rule is that an adjective following several nouns refers back to all of them, unless there is a verbal or semantic obstacle.

The word al-saw' (evil) in His words ﴿the thought of evil﴾ (zann al-saw') is read with a fatha on the sin by all ten readers ('ashara). As for His words ﴿the evil turn of fortune is upon them﴾, it is also read with a fatha by the majority of readers. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr alone read it with a damma on the sin. In the basic language, the fatha and damma forms are synonyms, and both mean what is disliked, the opposite of joy. They are two dialects, like al-karh and al-kurh, al-d'af and al-du'f, al-darr and al-durr, and al-ba's and al-bu's. This is reported from al-Kisa'i, and al-Zamakhshari followed him. Al-Jawhari clarified that the fatha form is a verbal noun (masdar), while the damma form is a noun of the verbal noun (ism masdar). However, usage has made the fatha form predominant when it is an adjective for something blameworthy whose qualified noun is attached to it, as in this verse and in His words ﴿and they wait for misfortunes to befall you; upon them is the evil turn of fortune﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98] in the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah). The damma form has become predominant for the thing that is itself evil.

[Page 154]

Therefore the attribution of zann (thought) to al-saw' is an attribution of a qualified noun to its adjective.

The intended meaning is their thought about God: that He has not promised the Messenger (ﷺ) victory, nor commanded him to go out for the 'umrah, nor decreed victory for the Messenger (ﷺ) because of the smallness of his followers and the might of his enemies. This is an evil thought about the Messenger (ﷺ), and this fits the reading with a fatha.

As for the evil turn of fortune (dA'irat al-saw') in the reading of the majority, it is the turn of fortune that brings evil upon those who think such thoughts, as shown by His words ﴿upon them﴾. It does not matter that it may be praiseworthy in the view of the believers, since this is not the place to explain that. The attribution is like the attribution of zann al-saw'. As for the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, the attribution of the damma-form dA'irah is an attribution of nouns, meaning the turn of fortune specific to evil and constantly accompanying it, not an attribution of a qualified noun.

Neither of their readings carries any additional distinction over the reading of the majority. Rather, they combine both usages: the first saw' with a fatha is required, and the second with a damma is permissible but not preferred. The difference is a difference in transmission.

The sentence ﴿upon them is the evil turn of fortune﴾ is a supplication or a threat. That is why it is in the nominal form, since it is suitable for that, unlike the sentence ﴿and God became angry with them, and cursed them, and prepared for them﴾, which is a report of what they committed of evil deeds. So the use of the past tense there is more appropriate.

This is a parallel to what came just before, except that here the attribute chosen is "Mighty" (ʿAzīz) rather than "All-Knowing" (ʿAlīm), because the purpose of mentioning the hosts here is warning and threat of defeat that will befall the hypocrites and the polytheists. Just as "To Allah belongs the hosts of the heavens and the earth" was mentioned earlier to indicate that the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) comes through the hosts of the believers and others, the mention here is for the threat of defeat. So the fitting attribute is "Mighty" (ʿAzīz), meaning that no conqueror can overcome Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 8–9:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner﴾ ﴿so that you [people] may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honor him, and glorify Him morning and evening﴾

When the discussion was about to move from the promise of victory and support, and what that entailed of related matters, to explaining what occurred in the incident of al-Hudaybiyah and conveying to everyone involved in that affair his due share, whether praise or otherwise, He preceded this with mention of the purpose of Allah in sending His Messenger ﷺ, so that it would serve as an introduction to the story. The wisdom of Allah – exalted is He – in sending him was mentioned, namely those qualities that have a particular connection to the event being discussed. Three attributes were mentioned: witness, bringer of good news, and warner. The attribute of witness was put first because the other two branch out from it.

The shahid (witness) is one who reports the truth or falsehood of someone in what he claims, or what is claimed against him. It has already occurred in His words ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these people?﴾ [al-Nisa: 41] in Surat al-Nisa, and His words ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

So the meaning is: We have sent you while you bear witness over the community regarding the conveying [of the message], such that those who oppose your law cannot be excused for what they opposed, and you bear witness over the nations. This testimony takes place in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Thus "witness" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), a hal of concomitance. What follows from the conveying to which he will testify is that he is a bringer of good news to the obedient and a warner to the disobedient, according to the degrees of disobedience.

The speech is an independent new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), and its emphasis with the particle of emphasis is for importance.

As for His words: ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honor him, and glorify Him morning and evening﴾.

The majority read the four verbs "li-tu'minu", "tu'azzirūhu", "tuwaqqirūhu", and "tusabbihūhu" with the second-person (ta') prefix in the four verbs. So the lam in "li-tu'minu" may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), indicating causation, and connected to the verb "arsalnaka" (We sent you).

The address may be to the Prophet ﷺ together with the community of the call, meaning: that you and those to whom you were sent as witness, bringer of good news, and warner may believe, and the intended meaning is belief in Allah. "And His Messenger" was inserted because the address includes the community, and they are commanded to believe in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; and because the Messenger ﷺ is commanded to believe that he is the Messenger of Allah, and for this reason he used to say in his tashahhud: "And I bear witness that

صفحة ١٥٦
Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger," and he said on the day of Hunayn: "I bear witness that I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger." It is authentically reported that he would repeat after the muezzin: "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

It is also possible that the address is specifically to people, and there is no difficulty in the coordination of "and His Messenger."

It is also possible that the speech ended at His words "and a warner," and the clause "so that you may believe in Allah" etc. is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah), and the lam in His words "li-tu'minu" is the lam of command, and the clause is a new sentence (istinaf) of command, as in His words, exalted is He: "Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend of that in which He has made you successors" in Surat al-Hadid.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with the ya' of the third person, and the pronouns refer to something known from the context, because witnessing, bringing good news, and warning necessarily require an object of relation, meaning: a witness over the people, and a bringer of good news and warner to them, so that they may believe in Allah, etc.

Ta'zir means support and reinforcement, and their support of Allah is like His words: "If you support Allah." Tawqir means honor.

Tasbih means speech that indicates the exaltation of Allah – exalted is He – above every deficiency.

The three accusative pronouns of the absent third person refer to the name of majesty (Allah), because the singular pronouns, although the preceding mention is of two names, indicate that the intended one is one of them. The indication for determining the intended referent is the mention of "and glorify Him," and because the conjunction of "and His Messenger" with the word of majesty is a counting of belief in the Prophet ﷺ as belief in Allah, so the intended is belief in Allah. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said in some reports from him that the pronoun in "tu'azzirūhu" and "tuwaqqirūhu" refers to His Messenger.

Al-Bukrah is the beginning of the day, and al-Asil is its end. These are a metaphor for covering all times with glorification and frequent recitation of it, as one says "east and west" to cover all directions.

It has been said that tasbih here is a metaphor for the obligatory prayers, and the statement regarding "morning and evening" is the same.

A parallel of this verse occurred in Surat al-Ahzab, namely His words: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner﴾ [al-Ahzab: 45] ﴿and a caller to Allah by His permission, and an illuminating lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]

صفحة ١٥٧
So there were added to the attributes of the Prophet ﷺ there: "a caller to Allah by His permission, and an illuminating lamp," and the like of this was not mentioned in this verse in Surat al-Fath. The reason is that this verse in Surat al-Fath came in the context of refuting the doubt of those who doubted the matter of the truce, and those who denied the promise of victory and support, and praising those who were reassured by that. So from the attributes of the Prophet ﷺ only the original attribute was limited to, namely that he is a witness over both parties, and that he is a bringer of good news to one of the two parties and a warner to the other. By contrast, the verse in Surat al-Ahzab came in the context of clearing the Prophet ﷺ of the slanders of the hypocrites and disbelievers regarding his marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Harithah divorced her, they claiming she was his son's wife. So it was fitting to add to his attributes what indicates a distinguishing between what belongs to the qualities of perfection and what belongs to the illusions arising from false claims like adoption. Thus there was added that he is a caller to Allah by His permission, meaning he does not follow the claims and desires of people, and that he is an illuminating lamp by which whoever has the aspiration for guidance is guided, without affectation.

The hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As concerning the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Torah has already been mentioned in the tafsir of Surat al-Ahzab, so refer back to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is above their hands. So whoever breaks [his oath] only breaks it to his own detriment, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward.﴾

A beginning of the main purpose of this surah. This sentence is resumed (independent), and it is emphasized with the particle of emphasis for the sake of importance. The present tense in His saying "yubayi'unaka" (they pledge allegiance to you) serves to evoke the sublime state of the pledge, so that it appears as if it were occurring at the time this verse was revealed, even though it had already passed. This is like His saying, exalted is He, "wa yasna'u al-fulk" (and he was building the ark).

The restriction conveyed by "innama" (indeed/only) is a restriction of the act to its object, i.e., they pledge allegiance to no one but Allah. It is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i), on the claim that the ultimate aim and purpose of the pledge is the support of the religion of Allah and His Messenger. So the purpose has been placed in the position of the means, and it is claimed that they pledged allegiance to Allah, not to the Messenger.

Since the restriction is an emphasis upon an emphasis, as the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) said: I did not make the "inna" at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, since emphasis is achieved by other means; rather I made it for the importance of this report, so that two purposes are achieved thereby.

From this claim he moved to imagining that Allah, exalted is He, is pledged to by those who pledge allegiance, so the hand, which is among the attributes of the one pledged to (al-mubaya' bi'l-fath, i.e., the one receiving the allegiance), was affirmed for Him in the manner of imaginative representation (takhyiliyyah), like the affirmation of claws for the (personified) Death (al-maniyyah).

The form of the pledge was prepared so that hands would be mentioned after it, because the pledge is accompanied by the pledger placing his hand in the hand of the one receiving the pledge, as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"Until my right hand came to rest, not contending with him, in the palm of one of great strength, whose word is the decisive word."

What added beauty to this imagery is the mushakalah (correspondence in wording) between "yad Allah" (the hand of Allah) and "aydihim" (their hands), as al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah: "Mushakalah is among the rhetorical embellishments (muhassinat badi'iyyah)." Allah is exalted above having a hand and the marks of created things.

Thus the sentence "yadu Allahi fawqa aydihim" (the hand of Allah is above their hands) confirms the meaning of the sentence "Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah," which conveys that their pledge to the Prophet ﷺ outwardly is, in reality, a pledge from them to Allah. The sentence "the hand of Allah is above their hands" established and emphasized this, and for this reason it is detached from a conjunction particle.

The imagined hand is said to be "above their hands" either because attributing it to Allah requires honouring it with elevation above the hands of people, just as the giver is described as "upper" in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The upper hand is better than the lower hand; the upper hand is the giving one and the lower hand is the taking one." Or because the pledge used to be made by the pledger extending his palm in front of the one receiving the pledge, and the pledger placing his hand upon the hand of the one receiving it; so the description with superiority ("above") is part of the imaginative representation. This is supported by what is in Sahih Muslim: "When the people pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Umar was holding the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," i.e., 'Umar was placing the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the hands of the people so that he would not tire from moving it because of the large number of those pledging, which indicates that the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was placed upon the hands of those pledging.

In any case, mentioning "above" here is a tarshih (supporting elaboration) for the metaphor and an immersion in imaginative representation.

The origin of "mubaya'ah" (pledging allegiance) is derived from "bay'" (sale), so it is a mufa'alah form, because each of the two contracting parties is a seller. It was transferred to the meaning of a covenant of obedience and support. Allah, exalted is He, said: "O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with Allah..." [al-Mumtahanah: 12], and here it means a covenant of support and obedience.

This is the pledge which the Muslims pledged to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of al-Hudaybiyah under a tree of sumur (acacia), and they were one thousand four hundred according to most reports. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "or more." And from him: that they were fifteen hundred. And from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa: they were thirteen hundred. The first to pledge allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ under the tree was Abu Sinan al-Asadi.

It is called the Pledge of Ridwan (Good Pleasure), because of Allah's saying, exalted is He: "Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree" [al-Fath: 18].

The cause of this pledge was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan from al-Hudaybiyah to the people of Makkah to negotiate with them regarding allowing the Muslims to be free to perform 'umrah at the House. Then a rumour spread that 'Uthman had been killed, so the Prophet ﷺ resolved to fight them for that, and he called those with him to the pledge that they would not turn back until they engaged the people. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah used to say: "They pledged to him that they would not flee." Salamah ibn al-Akwa' and 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd said: "We pledged to him unto death." There is no contradiction between these two, because not fleeing requires steadfastness unto death.

None of those who had gone out with the Prophet ﷺ to al-Hudaybiyah stayed away from the pledge except 'Uthman, since he was absent in Makkah negotiating regarding the 'umrah. The Prophet ﷺ placed his right hand upon his left hand and said: "This is the hand of 'Uthman." Then 'Uthman came and pledged. And al-Jadd ibn Qays al-Sulami hid behind his camel until the people had pledged; he was not a hypocrite, but he was weak of resolve. The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "You are the best of the people of the earth."

The statement "fa-man nakatha fa-innama yankuthu 'ala nafsihi" (whoever breaks [his oath] only breaks it to his own detriment) is a consequence (mufarra') of the sentence "Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah," for when it disclosed the true nature of this pledge, that it is a pledge to Allah, by necessity, since it is a pledge to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in respect of his message from Allah, the matter of this pledge became great and weighty, both in fulfilling what the pledge was made upon and in breaking it.

Nakth (breaking) is like the untying of a rope. Allah, exalted is He, said: "And be not like her who unravels her thread after it has been strengthened into strands" [al-Nahl: 92].

Nakth has become predominantly used for the figurative undoing, such as nullifying a covenant.

The speech is a warning against breaking this pledge and a denunciation of it, because the condition relates to the future. The present form "yankuthu," with a dammah on the kaf, is the well-known reading, and the reciters agreed upon it. The meaning of "fa-innama yankuthu 'ala nafsihi" is that his breaking returns upon him with harm, as the particle "'ala" indicates.

"Innama" here is for restriction, restricting the breaking to the referent of "'ala nafsihi," so that the meaning is: he harms by his breaking no one but himself, and does not harm Allah in anything. For breaking a covenant does not free itself from the intention of harming the one broken with, so the restriction of reversal (qasr al-qalb) is employed, reversing the intention of the breaker onto himself rather than onto the Prophet ﷺ.

One says "awfa bi'l-'ahd" (he fulfilled the covenant), which is the dialect of Tihamah, and one says "wafla" without hamzah, which is the dialect of the general body of the Arabs; but only the first form occurs in the Qur'an.

They said: No one among those who pledged allegiance broke it.

My own view is that the cause of the pledge had ceased with the truce concluded between the Prophet ﷺ and the people of Makkah, and that this verse was revealed in the interval between the moment of the pledge and the conclusion of the truce; and the reward for fulfilment is obtained by intention, even if what they covenanted with Allah upon did not occur.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ruways from Ya'qub read "fa-sanu'tihi" with the nun of majesty, by way of iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person. The rest read it with the ya' of the third person, its pronoun referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah).

[Page 161]

When he had warned against breaking the pledge and encouraged fulfilling it, he followed this with mention of those who stayed behind from joining the army of the Prophet ﷺ when he set out for the ʿUmrah (lesser pilgrimage) of al-Ḥudaybiyyah. This was done by the Bedouins who were camped around Madinah, and they were six tribes: Ghifār, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ashja', Aslam, and al-Dīl. They had given him the bayʿah (pledge) to go out with him. Then, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wished to set out for the ʿUmrah, he called on those around Madinah to go out with him, so that the people of Makkah would be awed by him and would not prevent him from performing his ʿUmrah. But most of them held back from going out with him. Among the people of the pledge was Zayd ibn Khālid al-Juhanī, from Juhaynah. From Aslam, one hundred men went out with the Prophet ﷺ, among them Mirdās ibn Mālik al-Aslamī, the father of the poet ʿAbbās; ʿAbdullah ibn Abī Awfā; Zāhir ibn al-Aswad; Uhbān (with a ḍammah on the hamzah) ibn Aws; and Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ al-Aslamī. From Ghifār came Khufāf (with a ḍammah on the unpointed kh) ibn Ayma' (with a fatḥah on the hamzah, followed by a silent yā'). From Muzaynah came ʿĀ'idh ibn ʿAmr.

Most of them stayed behind from going out with him. At that time, faith had not yet settled in their hearts, but they were not hypocrites. After the Prophet ﷺ returned, they prepared excuses, claiming that their possessions and their families had kept them busy. So Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ of what they had concealed in their hearts, and He exposed their matter before they made their excuses. This is one of the miracles of the Qur'an, in the reports it gave of things before they occurred.

Thus the sentence is an independent new beginning (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī), prompted by the mention of fulfilling and breaking the pledge. It was completed by mention of those who stayed behind from the one calling them to the covenant.

The meaning is: they will say this when the Prophet ﷺ returns to Madinah, offering excuses while lying in them.

Al-mukhallafūn (with a fatḥah on the lām) are those who stayed behind.

They were called "al-mukhallafūn", meaning others left them behind, i.e., he left them behind him, that is, he made them stay behind him. This does not necessarily imply that they were permitted to stay; rather, the mukhallaf is simply the one who is left behind. It is said: "We left so-and-so behind" when they passed by him and abandoned him. They made their excuses before the Prophet ﷺ went out, so he excused them, unlike the Bedouins, most of whom stayed behind after being called to go out and did not make any excuse at that time.

Al-amwāl (possessions) refers to camels.

Ahlūn is the plural of ahl (family) in an irregular way, since it does not meet the conditions for the sound masculine plural with wāw and nūn or yā' and nūn. So it is counted among the forms attached to the sound masculine plural.

The meaning of ﴿fa-istaghfir lanā﴾ (so ask forgiveness for us): ask Allah for forgiveness for us, since they were believers. So this is a genuine request, because they were believers. But they thought that the Prophet's ﷺ seeking forgiveness for them would erase what they had concealed of breaking the pledge. They forgot Allah's knowledge of what they had concealed, like the behaviour of ignorant people. The Jews, for example, killed Zakariyyā out of fear that a supplication might come from him against them when they killed his son Yaḥyā. For this reason, their statement here is followed by Allah's words, ﴿Rather, Allah is ever Aware of what you do﴾, and so on.

The sentence ﴿they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

It is also possible that it is a comprehensive apposition (badal ishtimāl) of the sentence ﴿The ones who stayed behind will say to you﴾.

The meaning is: they are lying in what they claimed as an excuse. Their staying behind was only because they thought that the Prophet ﷺ intended to fight the people of Makkah, or that the people of Makkah would certainly fight him, and that the army with the Prophet ﷺ could not overcome the people of Makkah. It is related that they said: "He goes to a people who attacked him in his own home in Madinah," meaning the Battle of the Confederates (Ghazwat al-Aḥzāb), "and killed his companions, so he will fight them." They thought that he would not return to Madinah. This was due to the weakness of their certainty.

﴿Say: Who then can avail you anything against Allah if He intends you harm or intends you benefit? Rather, Allah is ever Aware of what you do.﴾

The Messenger ﷺ was commanded to say to them what would return their matter to Allah, to let them know that his seeking forgiveness from Allah for them does not compel Allah to forgive; rather, Allah does what He wills when He intends it. If He intends them benefit, He benefits them, and if He intends them harm, He harms them. It is part of sincere counsel to oneself not to get entangled in what does not please Allah and then ask Him for forgiveness, since He may not forgive them. The purpose of this is to frighten them about the punishment for their sin, since they stayed behind from the Prophet's ﷺ call to go out and lied in their excuses, so that they would increase their repentance and seize what is still possible, as indicated by His words after it, ﴿Say to those who stayed behind of the Bedouins: "You will be called to a people of great might"﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 16], and so on.

So the meaning of ﴿if He intends you harm or intends you benefit﴾ here is the intention that proceeds in accordance with His knowledge, namely His giving them benefit or His afflicting them with harm. In this statement there is a direction that

their staying behind was a cause of their deprivation of the virtue of witnessing the Pledge of al-Riḍwān, and of their deprivation of witnessing the Battle of Khaybar, through his prohibition of their presence there.

The meaning of "mulk" (power) here is capability and ability, i.e., no one can change what Allah has willed. A similar construction occurred earlier in His words ﴿Say: Who then can avail anything against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Maryam?﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 17] in Sūrat al-ʿUqūd.

The usual case in such a construction is to negate the ability to turn harm into good, as in His words ﴿And whomever Allah wills to test, you cannot avail him anything against Allah﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 41]. So, following the apparent usage, the expression would be limited to negating that anyone could avail them anything if Allah intended harm to them, without adding "or intended benefit for you." This addition is understood as intended for completeness and comprehensiveness. A parallel is ﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends you harm or intends you mercy?﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 17] in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb. Something close to this has already passed in His words ﴿Say: I possess no benefit or harm for myself except what Allah wills﴾ [al-A'rāf: 188] in Sūrat al-A'rāf, so refer back to it.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read ḍarran with a fatḥah on the ḍād, while Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with a ḍammah, and both have the same meaning. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar), so it may be intended here in the sense of the verbal noun, i.e., "if He intends to harm you or benefit you." It may also be in the sense of the object, like khalq (creation) meaning makhlūq (created thing), i.e., "if He intends for you what harms you and what benefits you."

The meaning of the connection of "intends" (arāda) to it is that it means "intends to deliver what harms you or what benefits you."

This answer contains no promise from Allah that He will forgive them, since the intent is to leave them in a state of fear so that they will increase their good deeds. It was intended to open with this ambiguity so as to cast fear into their hearts that they might not be forgiven. Then He follows it with His words ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 14], and so on, which is closer to encouraging hope.

The "bal" (rather) in His words ﴿Rather, Allah is ever Aware of what you do﴾ is a turning away (iḍrāb) to nullify their statement ﴿Our possessions and our families kept us busy﴾. With it, the content of His words ﴿they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾ is strengthened as confirmation, because it implies the nullification of their excuse. From the meaning of nullification, the clarification of the generality in His words ﴿Allah is ever Aware of what you do﴾ is achieved, since it conveys that He is aware of their lying in the excuse. Therefore He negated their excuse with the particle of negation.

The placing of "bi-mā taʿmalūn" (of what you do) before its complement is for the purpose of emphasizing the mention of this action of theirs. The referent of "what you do" is what they believed and what they harboured of the reasons for their staying behind from the Messenger's call. The Qur'an often calls belief "action." In His words ﴿Allah is ever Aware of what you do﴾ there is a threat and a warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 12:

﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made attractive in your hearts; and you thought an evil thought, and you were a people doomed to ruin.﴾

This clause is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of comprehension, i.e., a clause that elaborates on what precedes it) for the clause ﴿Nay, Allah has ever been, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [al-Fath: 11], meaning: Acquainted with what you knew, and among it is your thought ﴿that the Messenger and the believers would never return﴾.

The particle of negation (bal, "nay") is repeated for the sake of emphasizing the meaning of substitution. Likewise the verb of the substituted-from clause is repeated, and al-inqilab (انقلاب) means: returning to one's dwelling place.

(An) is a lightened form of (anna), whose noun is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n), and the verbal noun (al-maṣdar) occupies the place of the two objects of "you thought" (ẓanantum). The particle (lan), which conveys the continuity of negation, is used, and it is emphasized by the phrase "abadan" (never), because their thought was strong.

Al-tazyin (التزيين) is al-tahsin (making something appear good), and it is a metaphor (kinaya) for acceptance of that. That thought was made attractive in their belief only because they did not posit any other possibility besides it, namely that the Messenger ﷺ would return safe. Such is the nature of feeble minds and fallen souls: they take from the images through which events may be imagined only the image that appears to them at first glance. It appears to them first because it is the beloved image; then adornment takes hold of it in the intellect, so they neglect to posit any other and do not prepare for its occurrence. For this reason it has been said: "Your love of a thing makes you blind and deaf."

They used to say among their sayings: "Muhammad ﷺ and his companions are a morsel (akalah, with three fathas) of a head," as a metaphor for paucity, meaning that a single sheep's head would satisfy them, and they will not return. That is, they are few in comparison with Quraysh, the Ahabish, Kinanah, and those in alliance with them.
