And "evil thought" (ẓann al-sau') is more general than their thought that the Messenger ﷺ and the believers would not return. That is, you thought an evil thought about the religion and about those among the certain believers who remained, because they were certain of the annihilation of the people of al-Hudaybiyyah, and that the polytheists would prevail, then attack Medina with those tribes that joined them, so that the believers would be dismayed and would apostatize from the religion; that is the evil thought.
The word al-su' (السوء) with a fatha on the sin was mentioned just before in His saying "those who think evil thoughts about Allah" (ẓann al-sau').

Al-bur (البور) is a verbal noun like al-hulk in form and meaning, and similar to it is al-bawar with a fatha, like al-halak (ruin). Therefore it occurs as a description in the singular while the described noun carries the sense of the plural.

The intended meaning is spiritual ruin, which is the absence of good and benefit in the religion and in the Hereafter, similar to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they destroy themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42] in the surah "Bara'ah".

The insertion of the word "qawman" (a people) between "kuntum" (you were) and "bura" (doomed) serves to convey that ruin has become one of the constituents of their peoplehood, due to its intense pervasiveness over all of them, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Surely there are signs in that for a people who understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in surah al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101] in surah Yunus.

This is an interjected sentence between parts of the speech commanded in His words, "Say: Who then has any power against Allah on your behalf..." (al-Fath: 11) and the verses, and His words, "And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth" (al-Fath: 14). This interjection serves as a warning against their leading themselves, step by step, into the stages of doubt regarding the correctness of the Messenger's (ﷺ) actions, which could lead them to the depths of disbelief after faith. For their staying behind from going out with him, and what they gave as excuses for their reluctance in their own souls, and their showing a false excuse while concealing the opposite, all of this is circling around the sanctuary of doubt, close to falling into it.

The "mun" (من) here is conditional (shartiyyah). The explicit mention of the word "the disbelievers" (al-kafirin) in a context where it could have said "We have prepared for them a blaze" serves to add emphasis to the meaning of "whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger."

Al-sa'ir (السعير): the kindled fire, and it is one of the names of Jahannam (Hell).

[p. 166]

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wwills, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is a coordination (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Who could avail you anything against Allah?﴾ [al-Fath: 11], so it belongs to the parts of the speech. This is a shift from the warning that the clause ﴿Who could avail you anything against Allah?﴾ [al-Fath: 11] suggested, to raising their hopes of the forgiveness they had asked for. For this reason, harm was placed before benefit in the first verse, where it says ﴿if He intends harm for you or intends benefit for you﴾ [al-Fath: 11], so that the possibility of God intending harm for them would come to their minds first.

Forgiveness is mentioned first here, with His saying ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾, so that the sense of hope is firmly established in their souls, and they hasten to make up for what they missed.

This is a preparation (tamhīd) for their promised reward in His saying ﴿Say to those who stayed behind of the Bedouins: You will be called to a people of great might﴾ [al-Fath: 16], up to His saying ﴿if you obey, Allah will give you a good reward﴾ [al-Fath: 16].

He strengthened the hope of forgiveness with emphasis by His saying ﴿and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning that mercy and forgiveness are closer than punishment. For both of these there are places and degrees of nearness and distance, and intentions and circumstances, and the value of good deeds and bad deeds, ﴿Allah has encompassed them﴾ [al-Fath: 21] and has measured them with precise measure.

The phrase "whom He wills" in both places is a general statement about the will and its causes. It has been explained more than once in the contexts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and among that is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48].

This is a second resumption (*istinaf*, a new sentence that picks up the argument) following His words ﴿The rear-guard among the Bedouins will say to you: "Our possessions and our families kept us busy"﴾ [al-Fath: 11].

It is also an announcement to the Prophet ﷺ of what those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya would say. It relates to their staying behind from al-Hudaybiyya and their false excuse, and that they will regret their staying behind when they see the people of al-Hudaybiyya gathering the fruit of their expedition. It also confirms the falsehood of their excuse for staying behind: when they know that there are spoils from a fight that is not severe, they eagerly seek to go out, and their possessions and families do not preoccupy them. So if their excuse were true, they would not have eagerly sought to go out when they expected the spoils, and they would have turned to occupying themselves with their possessions and families.

Because this statement came from them out of a rash and eager desire, the phrase with *lak* ("to you") was not included with it, as it was in His words ﴿will say to you﴾ [al-Fath: 11] mentioned just before. This is because this is an eager and sincere statement, not a fabricated one meant to deceive the Prophet ﷺ, as you know from what was said earlier.

Their being described as Bedouins was dispensed with, because the definiteness of *al-mukhallafun* ("those who stayed behind") is definiteness by prior reference, meaning "those who stayed behind who were mentioned."

His words ﴿when you set out to gains to take them﴾ are connected to ﴿will say, those who stayed behind﴾ and are not the content of the saying.

*Idha* ("when") is a time adverb for the future. The use of the past tense verb after it, rather than the present, is a metaphorical usage to express certainty. *Idha* serves as an indicator of this, because it is specific to the future tense.

The "gains" in His words ﴿when you set out to gains﴾ refers to the going out to the expedition of Khaybar. It is called "gains" by metaphor, by a relation of the first to the thing (*'alaqat al-awwal*), like the use of "wine" in His words ﴿I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. In this metaphor there is a hint that they will be victorious in their expedition.

When the Prophet ﷺ returned from al-Hudaybiyya to Medina, he stayed there for the month of Dhu al-Hijja in the sixth year and some days of Muharram in the seventh year. Then he went out to the expedition of Khaybar. Those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya wanted to go out with him, but he prevented them, because Allah made the expedition of Khaybar a spoil exclusively for the people of the Pledge of Ridwan, since He had promised them a near victory.

His words "to take them" are an intensifying complement to the metaphor, and it hints that the gains are certainly theirs.

That is because Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ that He had promised the people of al-Hudaybiyya that He would compensate them, for not entering Mecca, with the spoils of Khaybar.

*Maghanim* ("gains") is the plural of *maghnam*, a noun derived from *ghanima*, meaning to obtain what has benefit for oneself. It is as though they named it *maghnam* by considering the spoil as resembling a place where there are sheep (*ghanam*), so it was given the form *mafal*.

His words "leave us" indicate that the Prophet ﷺ would prevent them from going out with him to the expedition of Khaybar, because Allah commanded him not to go out to Khaybar except with those who were present at al-Hudaybiyya. This was mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿Pharaoh said, "Leave me, let me kill Moses"﴾ [Ghafir: 26] in Surat Ghafir.

His words "let us follow you" are a quotation of their statement. It implies that they said this phrase in order to bring down the granting of their request, by showing that they would go out to the expedition of Khaybar as followers, that is, that they were content to be at the rear of the army, so their share of its spoils would be small.

"Altering the words of Allah" means contravening His revelation of commands, prohibitions and promises, as an honour for the fighters and as a discipline for those who stayed behind from going out to al-Hudaybiyya. So "the words of Allah" refers to what He revealed to His Messenger ﷺ of the promise to the people of al-Hudaybiyya of the spoils of Khaybar exclusively for them. The "words of Allah" here does not mean the Qur'an, since no Qur'an was revealed about that on that day. The people who were joined to the people of al-Hudaybiyya included those of the emigration to Abyssinia, whom the Prophet ﷺ gave a share by revelation.

As for what is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, that the "words of Allah" means His words ﴿Say: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me"﴾ [al-Tawba: 83], Ibn 'Atiyya rejected this, saying that it was revealed after this surah, and that these people who stayed behind were not prevented permanently. Rather, they were prevented from participating in the expedition of Khaybar, so that they would not share in its spoils. This does not match His words there, "You will never go out with me," and it contradicts His words in this surah, ﴿Say to those who stayed behind among the Bedouins: "You will be called to a people of great might, you will fight them"﴾ [al-Fath: 16], since that was revealed about the expedition of Tabuk, which was three years after al-Hudaybiyya.

The clause ﴿they want to alter the words of Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

The "wanting" in His words ﴿they want to alter the words of Allah﴾ is in its literal sense, because at that time, when they say "leave us, let us follow you," they will know that Allah revealed to His Prophet ﷺ to prevent them from participating in the conquest of Khaybar, as their request to follow shows. So at that time they want to change what Allah commanded His Messenger when they say, "leave us, let us follow you," since following the army and going out at its beginning are the same in the intention of going out.

The majority read ﴿the words of Allah﴾. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *kalima Allah* ("the word of Allah"), a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *kalima*.

"Lan" (never), which conveys emphatic negation, is used to cut off their hopes of being permitted to follow the army going out to Khaybar. For this reason the complement of "you follow" is omitted, since it is known. "From before" is to be understood as: from before your request, which you are making. Allah had informed about what they would say when He said ﴿then they will say, "Rather, you envy us"﴾. They said this after about a month and a half. So when the Muslims preparing to go out to Khaybar heard their statement, they said, "Allah had informed us at al-Hudaybiyya that they would say this."

"Bal" (rather) here is for the retraction of the Messenger's ﷺ words ﴿you will never follow us﴾. It is a retraction of nullification arising from a sudden surge of anger mixed with ignorance and bad judgement. That is, it is not that you are guarding the command of Allah, but rather that you do not want us to share the spoils with you, out of envy of us for what we obtain of the spoils.

*Hasad* (envy) is the dislike that another should attain a particular or general good, whether accompanied by a wish that it pass to oneself or not. So "envy" here is meant as eagerness to have the spoils alone and dislike of sharing in them, lest the shares of those who dislike it be diminished.

Envy was previously discussed in His words ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty﴾ [al-Baqara: 90] and in His words ﴿out of envy from themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 109], both in Surat al-Baqara.

The pronoun of the nominative ("you") is meant to refer to the people of al-Hudaybiyya. They attributed envy to them, because they thought that the answer of preventing them was due to the people of al-Hudaybiyya's dissatisfaction with their sharing in the spoils. It should not be assumed that they meant by that pronoun to include the Prophet ﷺ, because those who stayed behind were believers who would not accuse the Prophet ﷺ of envy. For this reason Allah nullified their words with the nullifying retraction, saying ﴿Rather, they did not understand except a little﴾. That is, your saying this to them was not for the purpose of giving glad tidings of the spoils to the people of al-Hudaybiyya, but rather it was Allah's command and His right for the people of al-Hudaybiyya, and a discipline for those who stayed behind, so that they would be a lesson to others in what is to come. They thought it was collusion from the army of al-Hudaybiyya, because they did not understand His wisdom and its reason.

Allah negated understanding from them but not faith, because they were believers, but they were ignorant of the laws and systems of Islam.

His words "they did not understand" convey the negation of understanding from them, because the verb in a negative context, like an indefinite noun in a negative context, is general. Therefore He made an exception from it with His words "except a little," that is, except a little understanding. He described it as little because their understanding was limited to obvious matters of everyday affairs and did not penetrate to important matters and subtle meanings. Among this is their thought that they were being deprived of joining the army of the expedition of Khaybar, arising from envy.

In this assumption they followed the well-known practice of people of narrow outlooks and petty souls, who judge the deeds of people of perfection by the measure of what they find of motives for their own deeds and the deeds of their associates.

"Little" is a description of the omitted exception, and the implied reading is: except a little understanding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 16:

﴿Say to the desert Arabs who were left behind: "You will be called to face a people of great might; you will fight them, or they will submit. If you obey, Allah will give you a good reward, but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment."﴾

This is a transition to reassuring those who were left behind: that they will obtain spoils in future campaigns. This is so that they know that their exclusion from going out to Khaybar with the army of Islam does not mean that Islam has been withdrawn from them, but rather that it is for a wisdom of linking effects to their causes, in accordance with the wisdom of the Shari'ah. Thus it is an exclusion specific to one particular event, as was mentioned just above. And that they will be called after that to fight a disbelieving people, as the groups of Muslims are called. So mentioning this in this context is bringing joy after sadness, so as to remove from them the breaking of their hearts resulting from the exclusion. In this good news there is also an opportunity for them to make up for what they incurred of staying behind at al-Hudaybiyah. All of this indicates that they had not departed from faith. Do you not see that Allah did not treat the hypocrites who concealed disbelief with this kind of treatment, in His saying ﴿So if Allah brings you back to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me. You were pleased with sitting idle the first time, so sit with those who stay behind."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]

He repeated the description "from among the desert Arabs" here to make clear that this statement is aimed at those concerning whom His saying was revealed: ﴿The desert Arabs who were left behind will say to you: "Our possessions and our families kept us busy."﴾ [al-Fath: 11], so that the listeners do not imagine that the meaning of "those who were left behind" is everyone who happens to lag behind.

The verb "sutad'awna" is followed by the preposition (ila) to indicate that it is implicitly containing the meaning of walking (going). This is a subtle distinction between the verb of calling being followed by (ila) and it being followed by (li-), as in your saying: "I called so-and-so for what befell me." Tarafah said:

"And if I am called to the great deeds, I will be among their defenders."
The two usages may interchange with some kind of metaphor and leniency.

As for the people of great might, it is clear that they are a people from among the Arabs, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿you will fight them, or they will submit﴾ indicates that fighting will not be lifted from them except if they submit. This is a ruling only in the case of fighting the polytheist Arabs, since the jizyah is not accepted from them.

So it may be that the intended people are Hawazin and Thaqif. This is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, and that refers to the battle of Hunayn, which came after the battle of Khaybar. As for the conquest of Mecca, there was no fighting in it. And from al-Zuhri and Muqatil: they are the people of apostasy, because they are from the well-known Arab tribes for might, and that was at the beginning of the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. And from Rafi' ibn Khadij, that he said: "By Allah, we used to recite this verse: ﴿You will be called to a people of great might﴾ and we did not know who they were until Abu Bakr called us to fight the Banu Hanifah, so we knew that they were them." And from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, and al-Hasan: they are Persia and the Romans.

The clause ﴿you will fight them, or they will submit﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "you will be called", or an substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the content of "you will be called".

Page 172
The (aw) here is for expressing alternation between the two matters and specifying the states of being called: that is, you will be called to fight them and to their submission. This entails persevering in fighting them and continuing in it as long as they do not submit. **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 20:**

﴿God has promised you many spoils that you will take, and He has hastened this for you.﴾

This sentence is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question) arising from His words ﴿And He rewarded them with a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 18] and ﴿and many spoils that they will take﴾ [al-Fath: 19], since it is known that this was the conquest of Khaybar. It was therefore natural that they, and others, would think about other spoils awaiting them. So this statement was an answer to them, meaning: for you there are other spoils, of which none will be deprived, including those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyah. These are the spoils that would be obtained in the future conquests.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to the Muslims, following the address in His words ﴿when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ [al-Fath: 18], and it is not limited to those who pledged allegiance.

The promise of many spoils had already been made in what was revealed earlier in the Qur'an and in the words of the Messenger ﷺ, which he conveyed to the Muslims at the stages of his call to jihad.

The description of "spoils" by the clause ﴿that you will take﴾ serves to confirm the promise.

According to our preferred view that this surah was revealed all at once, the verb ﴿and He has hastened﴾ is used with reference to the future, metaphorically, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, meaning: He will hasten this for you. He made their reward the spoils of Khaybar as an "hastening" because it was close to the time of the promise. It is also possible that the revelation of this verse was delayed until after the conquest of Khaybar, so that it would serve as a completion of the promise verse before it, and that the Prophet ﷺ ordered its placement after it. We have pointed to this in our discussion of the beginning of this surah, but this is not transmitted.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿this﴾ refers to the spoils mentioned in ﴿and many spoils that you will take﴾ [al-Fath: 19]. It is pointed to in two ways, depending on the two considerations regarding the use of the verb in ﴿and He has hastened this for you﴾.

* * *

﴿And He withheld the hands of people from you﴾ is a reminder of a favour to them, a blessing they overlooked when they grieved over the conclusion of the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. It is the blessing of peace, meaning: He restrained the hands of the polytheists from them. For had they confronted them at al-Hudaybiyah with fighting, without discussing the reason for their coming, the Muslims would have returned exhausted after the fighting. And when the conquest of Khaybar was made possible for them, [it was also that] if they had fought with the people of Makkah, [the lives of] believing men and believing women who were in Makkah would have been destroyed, as His words indicate: ﴿Had it not been for believing men﴾ [al-Fath: 25], and so on.

So what is meant by "people" is the people of Makkah, following the Qur'anic usage of this term, which generally applies to them.

* * *

It has been said: what is meant is the withholding of the hands of the polytheist Bedouin Arabs from the tribes of Banu Asad and Ghatafan, who were allies of the Jews of Khaybar and came to support them when the Muslims besieged Khaybar. So God cast terror into their hearts, and they retreated.

It has also been said: the polytheists sent forty men to harm the Muslims at al-Hudaybiyah, but the Muslims captured them. This is what will come in His words ﴿and [He] withheld your hands from them﴾ [al-Fath: 24].

It has been said: [what is meant is] He withheld the hands of the Jews from you, meaning from your families and your offspring, since they were able to attack Madinah during the period when most of its people were absent at al-Hudaybiyah. But this view does not fit the general Qur'anic usage of the term "people."

The word *kaff* (withholding) means preventing the doer from an act he intended or had begun. It is derived from the noun *kaff* (hand), because the basic meaning of prevention is a push with the hand. One says: "He withheld his hand from such-and-such" when he prevented him from taking it with his hand.

The term *kaff* is used here metaphorically for diverting, meaning: God decreed the withholding of the hands of people from you, by creating the causes that turned them away from reaching you with harm, whether they intended it or not. The use of the verb for His decree is frequent in the Qur'an, since when there is no suitable verb in the speech of the Arabs to express divine meanings, the language was built upon the customary usage of people in their address, while most divine meanings came with the revelation of the Qur'an. Thus divine matters are expressed by the closest verbs to their meaning.

* * *

﴿And so that it may be a sign for the believers and that He may guide you to a straight path﴾

The apparent view is that the *waw* is conjunctive, and that what follows the *waw* is a reason, as the particle *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*) requires. Thus it must be a reason for something mentioned earlier in the wording, or a conjunction with a reason that preceded it.

It may be conjoined with some of the earlier reasons in His words ﴿that they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4], or with His words ﴿that He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens﴾ [al-Fath: 5], and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause, which, though long, was required by the connected transitions. The meaning is that God sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers for benefits that include their increase in faith, their deserving of Paradise, the expiation of their misdeeds, and the deserving of punishment by the hypocrites and polytheists. And so that tranquillity would be a sign for the believers, meaning a lesson for them and evidence of God's kindness towards them, and that His promise contains no misinterpretation.

What was meant by tranquillity being a sign is that it was the cause of a sign: when tranquillity came down into their hearts, their souls were calmed, so they were free to reflect and to reason, and the signs of God became clear to them. Thus the feminine pronoun in the verb agrees with its referent, which is tranquillity.

It may also be conjoined with a deleted reason that is suggested by the preceding speech. It was omitted so that the listener's mind would go in every possible direction in its estimation, to broaden the meaning. The estimation is: "He hastened this for you for purposes and wisdoms, and so that it would be a sign." This is a mention of the specific after the general that is implied.

Thus the estimation may be, for example: so that the hastening would come to you as a benefit in exchange for what you had hoped for from the gains of fighting the polytheists, and so that these spoils would be a sign to the believers among you, and to those who recognise through them that they are in the position of His special care, that He fulfils for them what He promised, and that He guarantees for them the promised victory, just as He guaranteed them the near spoils and the near victory. That sign increases the believers in strength of faith. In this case the pronoun in (*litakuna*, "that it may be") refers to (*hadhihi*, "this"), on the basis that it is the reason. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the qualities indicated by the whole of His words ﴿He has hastened this for you and withheld the hands of people from you﴾, so that the meaning of His words ﴿and so that it may be a sign for the believers﴾ is for many purposes, among which are those already mentioned, and among which is the safety of the Muslims at a time when they were most in need of preserving their strength rather than fighting the polytheists, saving it for the future.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) considered the clause ﴿and so that it may be a sign for the believers﴾ to be a parenthetical clause (*i'tiradiyyah*). According to this, the *waw* is parenthetical and not conjunctive, and the pronoun in (*litakuna*) refers to the single instance of the verb "withheld" (*kaff*), meaning "one withholding" (*kaffah*).

He conjoined to it: ﴿and that He may guide you to a straight path﴾, which is another wisdom, meaning: so that by this there may be removed from you the distress and grief that had entered you, and your souls would be freed to perceive the pure good that lies in the matter of the treaty, and to rely on the promise, so that you would be certain that this is the truth, and thus you would increase in certainty. It is also possible that the verb (*wa-yahdiyakum*, "and He may guide you") is used in the sense of continuing upon guidance, which is the faith they already had earlier, in the manner of His words ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 136], according to one of two interpretations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 21:

﴿And others, over which you had no power, but Allah has already encompassed them; and Allah is ever Competent over all things.﴾

This is the conjunction of one sentence to another. His saying "others" (ukhrā) is a subject (mubtada') qualified by the sentence "over which you had no power," and the predicate (khabar) is his saying "Allah has already encompassed them."

The whole sentence is conjoined to the sentence "Allah has promised you many spoils" (maghānima kathīrah). So the word "others" (ukhrā) is an attribute of an omitted noun indicated by "spoils" (maghānim) in the sentence before it. That is, they are another kind of spoils, difficult to obtain. The meaning of "spoils" requires those who take spoils, so it is known that they are for them, that is, other than those which Allah promised them. That is, these were not promised to them by Allah. We have not made "and others" (wa-ukhrā) a conjunction to his saying "these" (hadhihi), a conjunction of a singular to a singular, since the intended meaning is not one spoil but many spoils.

The meaning of "over which you had no power" is that they are described by your lack of power over them. Since the sentence "over which you had no power" is an attribute of "others," the content of the sentence does not imply that they attempted to obtain them and were unable; rather the meaning is that their attribute is your lack of power over them, so your desires were not attached to taking them.

Ihata (encompassing), with a hamza, means making a thing a wall (hā'iṭ), that is, a guard. Its original hamza is for making, and by usage it became intransitive. Its meaning: it comprised it and left it no way of escape, so it indicates intense power over it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unless you are encompassed [by enemies]﴾ [Yusuf: 66], that is, unless you are overpowered with an overpowering by which you cannot bring him.

So the meaning is: Allah has power over them, that is, He has power over them and made them yours, by the indication of His saying before it, "over which you had no power." The meaning: and spoils of others over which you had no power to obtain, Allah has already had power over them, that is, He will bring them to you.

Otherwise there would be no benefit in informing them that Allah has power over what they had no power over, since they do not ignore that. That is, Allah has encompassed them for your sake. In the meaning of encompassing there is an allusion that they are like a thing encompassed from all its sides, so its place does not escape them; they are made like something hidden for them.

For this reason it was appended with His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever Competent over all things﴾, since it is a matter established in their knowledge.

The apparent construction would have been the pronoun of "the people," saying, "If they had fought you," but He turned away from that to the apparent noun because of what the relative clause contains of an indication of the basis for the predication, namely that disbelief is the cause of turning their backs in their fighting against the Muslims, as a preparation for His saying, "the Sunnah of Allah which has passed before."
