**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 48, verse 24:**

﴿It is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah, after He had given you victory over them. And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause "and He restrained the hands of the people from you." This restraint is other than the restraint mentioned in His words "and He restrained the hands of the people from you."

The placing of the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate serves to affirm exclusivity, that is, restriction (qaṣr). The meaning is: He did not restrain them from you, nor you from them, except Allah the Exalted, not you and not them. For they wished evil upon you, and you, when you surrounded them, wished to kill them or take them captive. The motives for their hands reaching toward you, and yours reaching toward them, were abundant. Had Allah not placed barriers preventing both sides, you would have become entangled in fighting. He restrained their hands from you by alerting you to them before they could surprise you, and He restrained your hands from them when He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to pardon them and release them.

The meaning of "restraint" (kaff) was already discussed in His words, "and He restrained the hands of the people from you," earlier.

The meaning is that neither party refrained from attacking the other of its own accord. Rather, that was due to causes that Allah, the Exalted, brought about, because He willed that there be no fighting between them. This is a second favour, like the favour mentioned in His words "and He restrained the hands of the people from you."

This verse points to a restraint from fighting that Allah facilitated out of kindness toward the Muslims and to preserve their strength at a time when they needed it, after the battle of Badr and the battle of Uhud. The early exegetes agreed that this restraint occurred at al-Hudaybiyyah. This points to what has been narrated through various chains, some of which are in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi, where he said: "It is a sound hadith." In some versions there are additions beyond others: "A group of polytheists, estimated at six, or twelve, or thirty, or seventy, or eighty, armed, descended to al-Hudaybiyyah intending to take the Muslims by surprise. The Muslims became aware of them and seized them without battle. The Prophet (ﷺ) then commanded their release." This took place during the days when envoys were going back and forth between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the people of Makkah. Perhaps the Prophet (ﷺ) released them to avoid anything that would disturb the peace of the truce.

The pronouns of the third person refer to "those who disbelieved" in His words "And if those who disbelieved had fought you." The reason they refer to them, although the people whose hands Allah restrained were a different group from those mentioned in "And if those who disbelieved had fought you," is that the customary usage of the Arabs is that what some members of a people do is attributed to the people as a whole, without distinction. This was discussed earlier in Surah al-Baqarah in His words "And when We took your covenant."

As for His words (﴿in the valley of Makkah﴾): the apparent sense of the lexicon al-Asas is that the literal meaning of *baṭn* is the belly of a human or animal, and that its use for the lower part or the middle part of a thing is metaphorical (majāz). Al-Raghib said: "*Baṭn* is also used for the lower direction, while *ẓahr* is used for the upper. It is said *baṭn al-wadi* for its middle." The well-known usage of the word *baṭn* when it is added to a place is to mean the middle of that place, as in the words of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

*Among a band of youths of Quraysh, one of whom said, when they had embraced Islam, in the valley of Makkah: "Depart!"*

That is, in the middle of the sacred city. The one who said "Depart!" was ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab or Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib. However, the meaning of this in this verse is not clear, because it is not known that a confrontation between the Muslims and the polytheists occurred in the middle of Makkah that would have led to fighting, such that they would be granted the favour of having the hands of some restrained from others. Everything that happened and might have led to fighting occurred at al-Hudaybiyyah.

The majority of exegetes understood *baṭn Makkah* in the verse to mean al-Hudaybiyyah, using *baṭn* in the sense of the lowest part of a place. Al-Hudaybiyyah is near Makkah. It lies within the area of the non-sacred territory (ḥill), and part of its land is within the sacred precinct (ḥaram). It lies on the road between Makkah and Jeddah, and it is nearer to Makkah. Today it is known by the name al-Shumaysi. They took the verse to refer to the story mentioned in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and others, through various narrations, which is what we mentioned above. Some of them added to that story that the army of the Muslims pursued the enemy until they entered the houses of Makkah, killing and capturing some of them. In that case, *baṭn Makkah* would be understood in its well-known usage. But this report is confused (mudtarib) and contradicts the apparent sense of His words "He restrained their hands from you and your hands from them." Others made the interpretation even more remote, holding that the verse was revealed concerning the conquest of Makkah. This does not fit the context of the surah, and it contradicts the words of the early exegetes, who knew best what was intended. All of this is based on the premise that the preposition *bi-* in His words (﴿in the valley of Makkah﴾) is connected to the verb *kaffa* (restrained), meaning that the restraint occurred in the valley of Makkah.

In my view, it is also permissible that *bi-baṭni Makkah* be a stationary adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) functioning as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronouns in *ʿankum* and *ʿanhum*, and that it is a hypothetical circumstance (ḥāl muqaddarah). That is: "if you had been in the valley of Makkah," meaning, if the truce had not taken place, and you had entered as combatants, as the Muslims who disliked the truce desired, as was mentioned earlier. In that case, the use of *baṭn Makkah* follows the common usage, meaning in the middle of the city of Makkah.

Therefore the root *ẓafar* (victory) was chosen in His words "after He had given you victory over them," rather than saying "after He had given you help (naṣr) over them." This is because *ẓafar* means attaining the desired goal, and so it does not necessarily imply that there was a battle. Thus *ẓafar* is more general than *naṣr*. That is: after He had granted you what benefits you, namely the truce of peace and that you would return to ʿumrah in the following year.

The reason this place is identified by this idiomatic construction (iḍāfah) is to point out that the group of polytheists descended from the sacred territory of Makkah when they came down from the mountain of al-Tanʿim, which is part of the sacred precinct, and they were helpers of the people of Makkah.

The phrase "after He had given you victory over them" is connected to the verb *kaffa* in terms of its governing the coordinated object, that is, "and your hands from them," because this is the restraint that occurred after the Muslims gained victory over the group of polytheists, according to that narration. The context is clear from His words "after He had given you victory over them." This points out that the restraint of some of them from others was for the Muslims, after they had gained the upper hand over the enemy and granted them mercy once they were in control of them.

Thus *aẓfaraKum* is followed by *ʿalā* (over), because it is used in the sense of *ayyadakum* (supported you). Otherwise, its proper construction would be with *bi-*.

The clause "And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do" is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to the preceding clauses. *Baṣīr* here means "knowing of visible things," that is, knowing your deeds when you surrounded them and brought them to the Prophet (ﷺ), thinking that you would kill them or take them captive.

The majority read *taʿmalūna* with the second-person address (tāʾ al-khiṭāb), but Abu ʿAmr alone read it with the third-person (yāʾ al-ghaybah), meaning, knowing what they do of descending upon you while you were heedless, hoping to be able to overcome you. In both readings there is an elliptical omission (iktifāʾ): "Allah is ever Seeing of what you do and they do," or "of what they do and you do." This is because His words "He restrained their hands from you and your hands from them" indicate an action on the part of each group. That is, He knew your intentions and restrained them, for the wisdom of preserving your strength and your good reputation among the tribes of the Arabs, and so that the polytheists would find no pretext to accuse you falsely.

[p. 187]

**Him (هُمُ) are those who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering held back from reaching its place of sacrifice.** ﴿هُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وصَدُّوكم عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ والهَدْيَ مَعْكُوفًا أنْ يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ﴾

This is a *isti'naf* (a resumptive new sentence, a sentence that begins a fresh topic) which shifts the discourse away from the praise of the believers who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what they gained by that pledge: the pleasure of Allah Most High, His reward of the Hereafter, the good of this world both immediate and deferred, and the guarantee of victory for them in fighting the polytheists. It also moves to what He prepared for them of the causes of victory, and to the reproach of the polytheists for the disgrace they committed, namely barring the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque and barring the offering from reaching its people. This is a stigma upon them among the Arabs, who are the most entitled of people to honour those who perform *'umrah* (the minor pilgrimage). They claim to be the people of the Sacred Precinct of Allah, its visitors and its venerators. It had been their custom to accept every visitor to the Ka'bah from all religious communities. So they have no excuse for preventing the Muslims, but partisan zeal (*al-hamiyyah*) drove them to it.

The pronoun of the third person with which the sentence opens refers back to those who disbelieved, from His saying ﴿ولَوْ قاتَلُوكُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوَلَّوُا الأدْبارَ﴾ [al-Fath: 22], and so on in the verse.

The purpose of opening with their pronoun here is to draw the attention of the hearer to the news that follows, as when a story about a champion on one of the days of the Arabs is told, and then someone says: "'Antarah is the champion who defends."

The object of the relative clause (*al-silah*) is the phrase ﴿صَدُّوكم عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. The mention of (*alladhina kafaru*, "those who disbelieved") is an *idmaj* (incorporation, the inserting of one description into another for a further purpose), serving to condemn them with the attribute of disbelief. This incorporation also has a subtle point: the description "those who disbelieved" has the status of a genus, so the relative pronoun takes the force of a definite noun with the definite article of the genus. Therefore the sentence ﴿هُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ confines the genus of disbelief to this group, for the purpose of emphasis, because of their perfection in disbelief, by barring those who performed *'umrah* from the Sacred Mosque and by barring the offering from reaching its place of sacrifice.

*Al-hady* (the offering) is what is brought as a gift to the Ka'bah from the livestock. It is a noun used in the sense of the verbal noun (*ism al-masdar*), and for this reason it is used in the singular and plural alike, as the verbal noun is. He, Most High, said: ﴿والهَدْيَ والقَلائِدَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97], meaning the livestock that is offered and their garlands. Here it is used in the plural sense.

*Al-ma'kuf* is the passive participle of *'akafa*, because one who is made to stay in a place is made to remain there. It is said: *'akafahu*, so he remained (*fa-'akafa*). It is used intransitively and transitively, according to Ibn Sayyidah and others, just as it is said: *raja'ahu fa-raja'a* ("he turned him back so he turned back") and *jabarahu fa-jabara* ("he set him right so he was set right").

[p. 188]

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "I do not know of *'akafa* used transitively." He interpreted the passive form in His saying, Most High, (*ma'kufan*) as implying that *'akafa* carries the meaning of *habasa* ("to detain").

The benefit of mentioning this circumstance is to censure those who disbelieved for their barring of the Muslims from the House: they barred the offerings from reaching their place of sacrifice, so that the Muslims were compelled to slaughter their offerings at Hudaybiyah. By their deed they nullified a rite among the rites of Allah. Thus the mention of the circumstance portrays the state of the offerings as being held back.

The meaning of their barring the offering is that they barred those who owned the offerings from reaching the place of sacrifice at Mina. It is not meant that they barred the offerings themselves directly, because it is not reported that the Muslims offered the polytheists to let someone take their offerings to Makkah to be slaughtered there.

His saying ﴿أنْ يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ﴾ may be a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion) from *al-hady*. It may also be governed by a deleted preposition, which is *'an*, meaning: "from reaching its place of sacrifice."

*Al-mahill*, with a kasrah on the *ha'*, is the place of lawfulness (*mahall al-hill*), derived from the verb *halla*, the opposite of *harura* ("to be forbidden"). That is, it is the place where the offering may be slaughtered, and it is the place for which no other will suffice. For the one performing *'umrah* this is at Marwah in Makkah. For this reason, "when they were prevented, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to slaughter their offerings in their place, since it was impossible for it to reach Makkah, because the polytheists had prevented them from that." It is not established in the Sunnah that the Prophet ﷺ commanded them to aim at a particular direction for slaughtering in the land of Hudaybiyah. That is part of the tolerance of the religion. Therefore there is no profit in disputing the stipulation that the sacrifice must be in the land of the Sacred Precinct for one who is prevented (*al-muhsar*).

\* \* \*

﴿ولَوْلا رِجالٌ مُؤْمِنُونَ ونِساءٌ مُؤْمِناتٌ لَمْ تَعْلَمُوهم أنْ تَطَئُوهم فَتُصِيبَكم مِنهم مَعَرَّةٌ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ لِيُدْخِلَ اللَّهُ في رَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ لَوْ تَزَيَّلُوا لَعَذَّبْنا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾

[The verse] follows the reproach of the polytheists for the evil of their conduct, of disbelief and barring from the Sacred Mosque, and the desecration of the rites of Allah, with His promise to the Muslims of a near victory and abundant spoils. This dispels the arrogance of the polytheists in their strength and calms the eagerness of the Muslims for the hastening of the conquest. He makes clear that Allah restrained the hands of the Muslims from the polytheists, along with what He had established just before, in His saying ﴿ولَوْ قاتَلُوكُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوَلَّوُا الأدْبارَ ثُمَّ لا يَجِدُونَ ولِيًّا ولا نَصِيرًا﴾ [al-Fath: 22].

[p. 189]

﴿لَوَلَّوُا الأدْبارَ ثُمَّ لا يَجِدُونَ ولِيًّا ولا نَصِيرًا﴾ [al-Fath: 22]. That is, He did not command the Muslims to fight their enemy when they barred them from the House, because He willed the mercy of a group of believing men and women who were among the polytheists and whom the Muslims did not know. He also protected the Muslims from falling into calamities resulting from the destruction of their brothers. So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿ولَوْ قاتَلَكُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوَلَّوُا الأدْبارَ﴾ [al-Fath: 22], or to the sentence "He is the One who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them," and so on. Whichever is the case, it is a parenthetical statement (*kalam mu'taridh*, an interjected clause) between the sentence ﴿هُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وصَدُّوكم عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ and the sentence ﴿إذْ جَعَلَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا في قُلُوبِهِمُ الحَمِيَّةَ﴾ [al-Fath: 26].

The composition of this verse is marvellous in its two styles of expansion (*ital-ab*) and concision (*ijaz*), in its variety of transitions, and in the elegance of its words.

*Lawla* (if not) indicates the prevention of one thing because of the existence of another. That is, the punishment of the disbelievers was prevented because of the existence among them of believing men and believing women. What follows *lawla* is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is deleted, according to the customary manner of deleting it after *lawla* when the prevention of its answer is tied to the existence of its condition in an absolute way, not restricted by any circumstance. So the estimate is: "And were it not for believing men and believing women [existing]," as is indicated by His saying after it: ﴿لَوْ تَزَيَّلُوا﴾, meaning: "if they had not been existing among them." That is, the existence of these is the very thing for the sake of which the occurrence of the content of the answer of *lawla* was prevented.

The qualification of the men and women with faith indicates that their existence, which prevented the occurrence of the content of the answer, is the existence described by the faith of its owners. Yet the prevention is not tied to the existence of faith, but to the existence of the believing men and women themselves among them.

Likewise His saying ﴿لَمْ تَعْلَمُوهُمْ﴾ is not a predicate but a second description, since it is not the point of the benefit.

As for the conjunction of "believing women" to "believing men," although the existence of the believing men alone suffices to link the prevention of the answer to the condition, and although one could have said "and were it not for the believers," it is because the masculine plural in the terminology of the Qur'an generally includes women. Yet specifying women by mention is more fitting to the meaning of the absence of blame by their being killed, and to the meaning of the mercy of Allah being attached to them.

[p. 190]

The meaning of ﴿لَمْ تَعْلَمُوهُمْ﴾ is: you did not know their faith, since they had come to faith after the departure of the Prophet ﷺ as an emigrant.

From Junbudh (with a *jim* with a *damma*, a silent *nun*, a *ba'* with a *damma*, and a *dhal* with a dot), son of Sab' (with an unpointed *sin* with a *fatha*, and a *ba'* with a *damma*; it is also said *Sibā'* with a *kasra* on the *sin*). It is said that he was an Ansari, and it is said that he was a Qari, a Companion. He said: "They were seven men, of whom were named al-Walid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Salamah ibn Hisham, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, and Abu Basir the Qurashi. I have not found the name of the seventh. Umm al-Fadl, wife of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, was counted [among the women], and I suppose that the second of them is Umm Kulthum daughter of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who joined the Prophet ﷺ after he had returned to Madinah." And from Hajar ibn Khalaf: "Three men and nine women." The wording of the verse requires that the women be more than two.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿لَمْ تَعْلَمُوهم﴾ is that it covers both the sense of not knowing their persons and the sense of not knowing what is in their hearts. The first indicates that many of you, from among those present at Hudaybiyah from the people of Madinah and those with them from the Bedouins, did not know their persons, and so did not know who among them was a believer, even though the emigrants (*al-muhajirun*) knew them. The second indicates that they did not know what was in their hearts of faith, or what they had produced of faith after separating from them. That is, the whole army of emigrants and Helpers (*al-Ansar*) did not know all of that.

*Anna tatu'uhum* ("that you trample them") is a *badal al-ishtimal* from "men" and what is conjoined to it, or from the pronoun in the accusative in *lam ta'lamuhum*, meaning: "were it not that you would trample them."

*Al-wat'* is treading with the foot. It is used metaphorically for annihilation and destruction. Al-Harith ibn 'Ulbah al-Dhuhli combined both meanings in his saying:

*"You trampled us with a trampling, out of rage,*
*A trampling of one shackled, the root of the herb growing wild."*

*Al-isabah* is the reaching of what strikes.

The *min* in His saying *minhum* ("from them") is for a metaphorical starting point which returns to the meaning of causation: that is, there would reach you because of them and on their account a calamity (*ma'arrah*) which you would have been wary of its reaching you, had you known them.

[p. 191]

*Al-ma'arrah* is a noun of place or instance formed with the *mim* from *'arrahu*, when it befalls him: that is, it strikes him with what he dislikes and what is hard on him, whether harm, penalty, or evil talk. So here it gathers what would reach them if they inflicted damage on the Muslims: the blood-money for slain persons, the penalty for damages, the sin that falls upon the killers if they did not verify concerning the one they killed, and the evil talk the polytheists would spread among the tribes, that Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions had not spared the people of their own religion from harm, in order to make the Arabs hate Islam and its people.

The *ba'* in *bi-ghayri 'ilm* ("without knowledge") is for accompaniment: that is, accompanied by the absence of knowledge. The phrase governed by it is attached to *tusibakum* ("would reach you"): that is, there would reach you because of them hardships you do not know of until you fall into them.

This is a negation of knowledge other than the knowledge negated in His saying *lam ta'lamuhum*, because the knowledge negated in *lam ta'lamuhum* is the knowledge that they are believers, and its absence is the cause of the destruction of the unknown people, on account of which the reaching of the calamity was a consequence. The knowledge negated a second time in *bi-ghayri 'ilm* is the knowledge of the reaching of the calamity from their trampling, which follows from not knowing the faith of the people destroyed; and it is the knowledge whose absence would be the cause of undertaking their destruction.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿لِيُدْخِلَ اللَّهُ في رَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("that Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills") is for causation. The thing caused is actual, not hypothetical. It is the existence of the condition of *lawla*, on account of which the prevention of its answer occurred. So the thing caused is the linking of the answer to the condition: were it not for believing men and believing women, you would have punished those who disbelieved. This linking is for the sake of the mercy of Allah toward whom He wills among His servants. For by this prevention He showed mercy to the army of the Muslims, by preserving them from a calamity that would have reached them, and by keeping for them their strength in persons and equipment until a known term. He showed mercy to the believing men and women by saving them from destruction. He showed mercy to the polytheists by sparing them, perhaps they would become Muslims, or most of them would become Muslims, as happened after the conquest of Makkah. And He showed mercy to those among them who became Muslims afterward by the reward of the Hereafter. So the mercy here includes both the mercy of this world and the mercy of the Hereafter.

"Whom He wills" embraces everyone whom Allah willed to show His mercy in this condition, in this world and in the Hereafter, or in both together.

He expressed it with *man yasha'* ("whom He wills") because it includes many categories, because of its brevity, and because it points to the wisdom which the will of Allah required in the mercy toward those people.

[p. 192]

The answer to (lawla) may be considered omitted, indicated by the answer to (law) conjoined to (lawla) in His words "law tazayyalu" (Had they been distinguished). It is also permissible to consider the answer to (law) as linked, on the basis of likening the contention between the two conditionals (lawla and law) to the fact that both conditionals return to one meaning, namely prohibition (imtina'). For (lawla) is a particle of prohibition due to existence (imtina' li-wujud), meaning it indicates the prohibition of its answer due to the existence of its condition.

(Law) is a particle of prohibition due to prohibition (imtina' li-imtina'), meaning it indicates the prohibition of its answer due to the prohibition of its condition. So the ruling of their two answers is one, namely prohibition, and only their conditions differ: the condition of (law) is negated, while the condition of (lawla) is affirmed.

The pronoun in "tazayyalu" refers to what is indicated by His words "wa-lawla rijalun mu'minun..." (and were it not for believing men...) etc., namely a mixed gathering in which there were believing men and believing women along with the polytheists, as indicated by His words "lam ta'lamuhum" (you did not know them).

Tazayyul is the reflexive (mutawa'a) of zayyalahu, when one removes him from a place; and zayyalahum means he removed some of them from others, i.e., separated them. He, exalted is He, said: "fa-zayyalna baynahum" (then We separated them). Here it carries the meaning of separation and distinction without regard to a reflexive relation to the action of an agent, because the forms of the reflexive (af'al al-mutawa'a) are very often used to express intensification, since an increase in the form indicates an increase in the meaning, and that is a principle of the principles of the language.

The meaning is: Had the believing men and believing women separated from the people of polytheism, We would have empowered the Muslims over the polytheists, and they would have punished those who disbelieved with the punishment of the sword.

The attribution of the punishment to God, exalted is He, is because He commands it and decrees victory for the Muslims, as He, exalted is He, said: "Fight them; God will punish them at your hands" (9:14), in Surah Bara'ah.

The "min" in His words "minhum" is partitive (li-l-tab'id), i.e., We would have punished those among them who disbelieved from that mixed gathering, now separated and distinguished, its believers from its disbelievers, i.e., when the gathering becomes pure polytheists alone.

The clause "law tazayyalu" to its end is an explanation of the clause "wa-lawla rijalun mu'minun" to its end, i.e., had it not been for the existence of believing men etc. blended into the community of the polytheists, not separated from them; had they separated, We would have punished the disbelievers among them.

He shifted from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in His words "la-'adhdhabna alladhina kafaru" (We would have punished those who disbelieved), in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 26:

Page 193
﴿When those who disbelieved had placed in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah). But Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and imposed upon them the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is ever Knowing of all things.﴾
(The phrase "idh" is an adverbial clause) connected to the verb "sadduukum" (they barred you). That is, they barred you in a manner for which they had no excuse and no cause to do so except the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance. Otherwise, the believers had come peacefully, honoring the sanctity of the Ka'bah, driving the offerings for the benefit of the people of the Sanctuary. It was therefore not sound judgment to prevent them from the 'umrah. But the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance had overshadowed their intellects, so they insisted on preventing the Muslims. Then the dispute between the two groups ended in a truce, on condition that the Muslims return this year, and that the polytheists would allow them to perform 'umrah in the following year, and that the two years were equal in their eyes. But they wanted to satisfy what was in their hearts of rancor against the Muslims.

So the attachment of this adverbial clause to the verb "sadduukum" implies the causation of the barring by its being the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance, in order to convey that the zealotry was firmly established in them, its effects appearing through them, among them the barring from the Sacred Mosque.

Al-hamiyyah (zealotry): al-anafah (disdain), that is, refusing something because one sees it as a humiliation for oneself. Its most common application is to arrogance without any justification for it; if it has a justification, it is "ibaa' al-dhaym" (refusal of oppression).

Since their barring the people from visiting the House was without right, because the House is the House of Allah and not theirs, the driving motive for the prevention was merely zealotry. Allah the Exalted said: "and they were not its guardians." And "ja'ala" is in the sense of "wada'a" (placed), as in al-Hariri's words in the final maqamah: "Make death before your eyes," and the poet's words:

"And kohl that is placed in the eye"

Page 194
The pronoun in "ja'ala" may refer to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying "that He may admit into His mercy" from His saying "We would have punished those who disbelieved." The turning from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun is an iltifat (shift).

"Those who disbelieved" is the first object of "ja'ala." "Al-hamiyyah" is a substitution of part (badal ishtimal) from "those who disbelieved," and "in their hearts" is in the place of the second object of "ja'ala." That is, they were characterized by zealotry, so it drove them to their actions, not observing any benefit or harm; likewise when they barred you from the Sacred Mosque.

"In their hearts" is also connected to "ja'ala," that is, He placed zealotry in their hearts.

His saying "zealotry of the Age of Ignorance" is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) for "al-hamiyyah." The purpose of stating it briefly and then in detail is to establish its meaning and confirm it, which would not be achieved had he said: "When those who disbelieved placed in their hearts the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance."

The attribution of "al-hamiyyah" to "al-jahiliyyah" is intended to belittle and disgrace it, for it is a trait of the people of the Age of Ignorance. This attribution is a blameworthy association in the terminology of the Qur'an, like His saying: "They think about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Age of Ignorance" [Al 'Imran: 154] and His saying: "Do they then seek the judgment of the Age of Ignorance?" [al-Ma'idah: 50].

The reverse of this is the attribution of "tranquility" to the pronoun of Allah the Exalted, an attribution of honor, because tranquility is among the noble morals, so it is a divine gift.

The conjunction of "fa-anzala Allahu sakinatahu 'ala rasulihi wa 'ala al-mu'minin" (then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers) with "idh ja'ala alladhina kafaru" (when those who disbelieved placed) implies that the believers wished to fight the polytheists and to enter Makkah for 'umrah by force, out of anger at their being barred from it; but Allah sent down tranquility upon them.

By "al-sakinah" is meant steadfastness and forbearance, that is, He placed deliberation in their hearts and turned hastiness away from them, so He protected them from meeting zealotry with anger and vengeance. They met zealotry with reason and steadiness, and in that there was much good.

Page 195
In this verse there are subtle rhetorical points: the contrast of "ja'ala" with "anzala" in His saying "When those who disbelieved placed in their hearts the zealotry" and His saying "then Allah sent down His tranquility." This indicates the nobility of tranquility over zealotry, because "inzal" (sending down) implies elevation. There is also the attribution of zealotry to the Age of Ignorance, and the attribution of tranquility to the Name of His Essence.

"He made them bind themselves to the word of piety" is conjoined to "Allah sent down His tranquility." That is, He made the word of piety binding upon them, not separating from it. That is, He linked them to the word of piety so that this would be the counterpart of His saying: "and they barred you from the Sacred Mosque" [al-Fath: 25]. For when He tied their barring of the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque to the clause in His saying "When those who disbelieved placed in their hearts the zealotry, the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance," with a tie that implies causation as we mentioned just above, He tied the Muslims' adherence to the word of piety to the sending down of tranquility into their hearts, so that the sending down of tranquility into their hearts, which is an inward matter, would have an effect on them in outward action, namely their adherence to the word of piety, just as the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance was what drove those who disbelieved to bar the Muslims from the Sacred Mosque.

The pronoun of object in "alzamahum" refers to the believers, because they are the ones for whom Allah compensated their anger with tranquility; and the Messenger of Allah had not been separated from tranquility before.

As for "kalimat al-taqwa" (the word of piety): if it is taken in the apparent meaning of "kalimah" (word), it is from the category of utterances, and the use of "kalimah" for speech is common. Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, it is a word he is saying" [al-Mu'minun: 100]. The word here is explained as the statement "There is no god but Allah." This was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b from the Prophet ﷺ, as related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: it is a gharib hadith. I say: in its chain is Thuwayr, also called Thawr ibn Abi Fakhitah, of whom al-Daraqutni said: he is matruk (abandoned), and Abu Hatim said: he is weak. Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like from Abu Hurayrah and Salamah ibn al-Akwa' with a marfu' attribution, and all their chains are weak. Its explanation by this was also related from a large number of the Companions. The meaning of His binding them to the word of piety is that He decreed for them steadfastness upon it: by its wording in speech and by its meaning in action, since the benefit of speech is the realization of its meaning. So the use of "kalimah" here is like its use in His saying: "And He made it a lasting word in his posterity" [al-Zukhruf: 28], meaning by it the saying of Ibrahim to his father and people: "Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me."

The attribution of "kalimah" to "al-taqwa" on this interpretation is a genuine attribution (idafah haqiqiyyah). The meaning of

Page 196
its attribution: that the word of testimony is the root of piety, for the foundation of piety is avoiding the worship of idols, and then from this branch all the branches of piety.

Other statements have been related in the interpretation of "kalimat al-taqwa" as another word from the good words, but these are interpretations that do not suit the context of the speech nor its composition. It is permissible to take "kalimah" in other than its apparent meaning, so that it is inserted (muqhamah), and its attribution to al-taqwa is an explanatory attribution (idafah bayaniyyah), meaning a word that is piety, and the meaning would be: "and He imposed upon them piety," in the manner of the insertion of a noun in the words of Labid:

"Until the year's end, then the name of peace be upon you both"

And from it is His saying: "Blessed is the name of your Lord" [al-Rahman: 78] according to one of the two interpretations of it. Included in piety is the beginning of the monotheism of Allah the Exalted.

It is also permissible that the word "kalimah" be used for the reality of a thing, its general meaning being like the use of "ism" (name) in the words of al-Nabighah:

"Zur'ah was informed, and foolishness is like its name, guiding to the strange of poetry"

This view is supported by what was related from Mujahid that he said: "The word of piety is sincerity." He thus made "the word" a meaning of piety. So the meaning according to these last two views is that they were characterized by piety and did not separate from it; "alzam" is borrowed for continuous accompaniment. These two views do not contradict the interpretation of "kalimat al-taqwa" as the word of testimony, related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for that would be an interpretation by a part of piety that is its most important part, that is, an interpretation by example.

It is also related from al-Hasan that the word of piety is fulfilling the covenant. In that case "alzam" would mean "ijab" (making obligatory): that He commanded them to fulfil what they had covenanted with the polytheists and not to break their covenant. For this reason the Muslims did not break the covenant until it was the polytheists who began to break it.

The waw in "wa kanu ahhaqqa biha" (and they were more deserving of it) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the accusative, that is: He imposed that word upon them in a state in which they were more deserving of it and worthy of it than those who did not adhere to it, namely those who did not accept monotheism, in the manner of His saying: "And indeed, it is a great thing, except for those whom Allah has guided" [al-Baqarah: 143].

Page 197
The verb "kanu" is used because it indicates that this deservingness is firmly established in them and occurred in the past time, that is, in the decree of Allah the Exalted.

The meaning: the souls of the believers were prepared to accept the word of piety and to adhere to it by what Allah had guided them to.

The one preferred over is implied, indicated by what preceded it, that is, more deserving of it than those who disbelieved and those whom Allah placed zealotry in their hearts, because Allah had decreed for them the readiness for faith, unlike those who persisted in disbelief.

"Ahl" (people) of a thing is its deserving one. The meaning is that they were the people of the word of piety, because it corresponds to their inner natures and to what their hearts had embraced.

This worthiness, like deservingness, varies among people, and whenever any of the polytheists is guided to Islam, his guidance indicates that this worthiness for Islam had been attained by him.

The clause "wa kana Allahu bikulli shay'in 'alimah" (and Allah is ever Knowing of all things) is a concluding clause (tadhyil), that is: that was preceded in the knowledge of Allah concerning that, within the generality of what the knowledge of Allah encompasses of things, in the course of His creation, in accordance with His knowledge.

[Page 198]

It is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers an implied question), arising from His words, "So Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers." It serves to dispel what had crept into the souls of a group of people: faintheartedness, doubt, or bewilderment. It also clarifies what Allah bestowed upon the people of the Pledge of Ridwan (*Bayʿat al-Riḍwān*) of worldly and otherworldly reward, and it resolves a confusion that had arisen for the people concerning a dream that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had seen. The reason is that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a dream before he set out for al-Ḥudaybiyah, or while he was at al-Ḥudaybiyah: that he and his companions had entered Makkah safely, and had shaved their heads and shortened their hair." Thus the dream was in general terms, containing no performance of Hajj or ʿUmrah, and shaving and shortening are appropriate to both.

[Page 199]

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related his dream to his companions, and they rejoiced at it and interpreted it as meaning that they would enter Makkah for their ʿUmrah, for which they had set out. When the treaty was concluded and the people prepared to return, some of the hypocrites raised the matter of the dream, saying: "Where is the dream? By Allah, we did not enter the Sacred Mosque, nor did we shave or shorten our hair!" Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to them: "The dream was not restricted to a particular time, and he will indeed enter." Then Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse.

The meaning is that the dream of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is true, that Allah revealed it to him, and that although it did not come to pass in that affair, it would be realized afterwards. The wisdom in Allah showing His Messenger ﷺ that dream at that time, and in the Messenger ﷺ informing his companions of it, seems to have been that Allah thereby placed in their hearts confidence in their strength and trained them in boldness against the polytheists in their own land, so that their hearts would be cleansed of the water of cowardice. For psychological ailments, when they afflict souls, do not fail to leave remnants of the disease for a period, just as the traces of illness remain in a diseased limb after recovery for a time, until the limb returns to its original strength after a suitable interval.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle *qad* (indeed) is to nullify the doubt of the hypocrites who said, "Where is the dream?" The meaning of "Allah has made His Messenger true in the dream" is that He showed him a true dream, since the dreams of the prophets are revelation; it therefore attains the sense of a report, and for this reason it is described as true.

This is an assurance to them that this will certainly happen, although at the time the verse was revealed it had not yet occurred, as indicated by His words "if Allah wills."

The transitive use of *ṣadaqa* (to make true) with a second object after its first object is in the accusative by the elision of the preposition, known as *ḥadhf wa-al-īṣāl* (dropping the preposition and transferring the verb's action), that is, the preposition is removed and the verb is made to govern the noun that followed it in the accusative. The original sentence was: "Allah made His Messenger true in the dream," like His words, "They were true to what they covenanted with Allah," [Qur'an 33:23].

The *bāʾ* in *bi-al-ḥaqq* (in truth) indicates accompaniment, and the phrase is a fixed adverbial (*ẓarf mustaqarr*) that stands as a qualifier of an elided verbal noun, meaning "a truth accompanied by reality." Or it may be a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the dream, after an elided verbal noun, meaning "a truth accompanied by..."

[Page 200]

*Al-ḥaqq* means the correct purpose and wisdom, that is, the dream was true and was constructed soundly, as I have just mentioned.

The clause "**Lata'dukhulunna al-Masjid al-Ḥarām**" (You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque) to its end may be an explanation of the clause "Allah has made His Messenger true," because the meaning of *la-tadkhulunna* (you will surely enter) is the confirmation of entering the Sacred Mosque in the future. It is thus understood that the dream was a report of an entry whose time was not specified, so it is true regarding what will be realized in the future. This is a reminder to those who did not perceive this and were certain that the dream of entering the mosque required their entering it at that time, although this is not implied by the dream. It was their duty to know that it was a promise whose appointed time had not been specified. Abu Bakr understood this when he said to them: "The dream was not restricted to a particular time, and he will indeed enter." And it has come in the Sura of Yusuf: "And he said, 'O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before,'" [Qur'an 12:100].

This clause is not an explanation of the dream, because the form of an oath does not suit that.

It is best that the clause "Lata'dukhulunna al-Masjid al-Ḥarām" be a resumptive explanatory clause (*istiʾnāf bayānī*) following the clause "Allah has made His Messenger true," meaning that this will certainly occur in the future. Therefore one should pause at His words "bi-al-ḥaqq" (in truth) so that the sense of resumption becomes clear.

His words "**in shāʾa Allāh**" (if Allah wills) are characteristically appended to a future report when its realization is distant. Do you not see that the one who is told, "Do such-and-such," and replies, "I will do it, if Allah wills," is not understood from his words to be doing it immediately or in the near future, but rather that he will do it after a time, while affirming that he will indeed do it?

For this reason they interpreted His words, exalted is He, in the Sura of Yusuf, "And he said, 'Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in safety,'" [Qur'an 12:99], as meaning that "if Allah wills" refers to the entering, with the security understood, because he said that when they had already entered Egypt. As for what is in this verse, it is the speech of Allah, so this interpretation does not suit it. It is not intended to be an escape from fulfilling a promise. This is one of the usages of the expression "if Allah wills." It is not like its usage in an oath, for there it has the sense of an exception (*thunyā*), because it stands in the place of the phrase "unless Allah wills," since the meaning of "unless Allah wills" is "non-occurrence of the action." But "if Allah wills," which stands in the place of "unless Allah wills," means "if Allah wills the action."

[Page 201]

The promised matter is true regarding their entry into Makkah for ʿUmrah in the seventh year, which was the ʿUmrat al-Qaḍiyya (the Makeup ʿUmrah). They entered the Sacred Mosque safely, some of them shaved their heads and some shortened their hair, without fear, since there was a covenant between them and the polytheists. This was the nearest entry after this promise. It is also true regarding their entry into the Sacred Mosque in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage (Ḥajjat al-Wadāʿ), where the absence of fear was more evident. As for their entry into Makkah on the day of the Conquest (Fatḥ), they were not in a state of iḥrām at that time. Mālik said in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, after relating the hadith of the killing of Ibn Khaṭal on the day of the Conquest: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not in iḥrām that day." And Allah knows best.

"**Muḥallilīna ruʾūsakum**" (shaving your heads) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in "āminīn" (secure), and "**wa-muqaṣṣirīn**" (and shortening) is coordinated with it. Shaving and shortening are a metaphor for the ability to complete Hajj and ʿUmrah, and this is part of the continuation of safety. This circumstance also reports what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw in his dream, meaning that whoever wishes to shave may shave, and whoever wishes to shorten may shorten. That is, fear will not hasten them to shaving so that they limit themselves to shortening.

The clause "**Lā takhāfūn**" (you do not fear) is in the place of a circumstantial clause. It may be an emphatic restatement of "āminīn" by a synonymous emphasis, to indicate that the security is complete and assured. It may also be a circumstantial clause that is newly established, on the basis that "āminīn" is the object of the verb "tadkhulunna" (you will enter), and that "lā takhāfūn" is the object of "āminīn," meaning "secure with the security of one who does not fear," that is, "you do not fear treachery." This implies that they will be stronger than their enemy who gave them safety. This points to the wisdom of delaying their entry into Makkah until the following year, when they would grow in strength and preparation, and it is more evident in their entry in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage.

The *fāʾ* (so) in His words "**Fa-ʿalima mā lam taʿlamū**" (so He knew what you did not know) is for the sequencing of the report, not the sequencing of what is reported, because Allah's knowledge precedes their entry and the dream that announced their entry, as mentioned earlier in His words, "So He knew what was in their hearts" [Qur'an 48:18].

In the choice of the verb *jaʿala* (He made) in this construction, rather than saying "He opened for you a near victory beyond that" or something similar, there is the indication that this conquest is a matter of wonder, and such a thing would not have occurred had Allah not brought it into being. The past form *jaʿala* is used to present the certain future as if it were past, or because *jaʿala* means "decreed." Here *dūna* means "other than," and *min* is either initial (indicating a starting point) or explanatory.

[Page 202]

The meaning is: He made a near conquest for you in addition to what He had promised you of entering Makkah safely. The first of this conquest was the conquest of Khaybar, which occurred before the ʿUmrat al-Qaḍiyya, and this near one is from the time of the treaty.

(Page 202)

﴿He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as Witness.﴾ This is a further confirmation of the truthfulness of the vision, since the One who sent His Messenger (ﷺ) with this religion would not have shown him a false vision. This sentence is therefore an emphasis on the certainty conveyed by the particle (qad) and the oath particle (lam) in His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth﴾. From this, the appropriateness of the pronoun and the relative clause in His saying "He is the One who sent His Messenger" becomes clear, because the relative clause generally conveys knowledge of the content of its clause.

The pronoun refers to the Name of Allah in His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. They know that the vision of the Messenger (ﷺ) is revelation from Allah. So He reminds them of these two known truths, at a time when they did not act in accordance with the requirement of knowledge of them, so doubts crept into them that are not fitting for one who knows that the vision of the Messenger is revelation and that the One who revealed it to him is the One who sent him. How then would He show him a vision that is not true? In this there is a reminder and a rebuke to the believers who were heedless of this, and an allusion to the hypocrites who introduced doubt into the hearts of the believers.

The preposition (bi) in (bil-huda) denotes accompaniment, and it is connected to "arsala" (sent). "Guidance" (al-huda) is used to refer to that by which guidance is achieved, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing﴾, and His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed, a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

"The religion of truth" is coordinated with "guidance" so as to include what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought of rulings, both their foundations and their branches, of what was revealed to the Messenger (ﷺ) other than the Qur'an, of every revelation expressed in words not intended as a miracle (i'jaz), or that was part of the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ).

It is also permissible that "guidance" means the foundations of the religion, from the belief of faith and the virtues of character by which the soul is purified, and that "the religion of truth" means the laws of Islam and its branches.

The lam in (li-yuzhirahu) denotes the purpose of the verb "arsala" and its complements. That is, He sent him with this so that He might make this religion prevail over all the divine religions that preceded it. For this reason (kullihi) is emphasized with the word "kull", because it carries the meaning of totality (al-jam').

The meaning of (yuzhirahu) is "to raise it high" (yuli'uhu). The root of "izhar" is derived from "zahara", meaning "to appear". It was used metaphorically (kinaya) for actual elevation, and then used figuratively (majaz) for honour, so "azhara-hu" came to mean "made it high", that is, to honour it above all religions. This is like His saying concerning the Qur'an: ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book and as a guardian over it﴾.

Since the purpose of His saying: ﴿He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance﴾ and so on is the testimony that the vision is true, He concluded the sentence with His saying: "and sufficient is Allah as Witness", meaning: the testimony of Allah to the truth of the vision suffices you until you see its fulfilment in its appointed time.

The discussion of the parallel of "and sufficient is Allah as Witness" was already given at the end of Surah al-Nisa'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 48, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Muhammadun is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces, the trace of prostration.﴾

When he (Allah) had established the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ in his vision, and the hearts of the believers were at rest, He followed that with praise of the rank of the Messenger ﷺ and commendation of the believers who are with him.

"Muhammadun" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "Huwa Muhammadun" (He is Muhammad). This pronoun, which is omitted, refers to his saying "rasulahu" (His messenger) in the verse before it. This is from the omission of the predicate (al-musnad), which al-Sakkaki described as "the omission that is customary," which occurs alongside the omission of the subject (al-musnad ilayh) and its counterparts. Al-Taftazani said in al-Mutawwal: Among it is their saying, after they mention a man: "A youth whose matter is such-and-such," and, when they mention the abodes or dwellings: "The encampment of such-and-such." Among the examples of al-Miftah for that is his saying: "So consider the two of them," i.e., sound reason and upright disposition, in the manner of his saying:

"I will thank 'Amr, if his death is delayed, for favours not bestowed, and if they are great"

"A youth who does not withhold his wealth from his friend, nor displays complaint when the sandal slips."

Since he did not say: "He is a youth."

This meaning is the most apparent here, since the intent is not to inform that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, but rather to specify who the Messenger of Allah is, after having applied to him the reports from His saying: "Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth" up to His saying: "that He may make it prevail over all religion." So the hearer is considered as one eager for a clarification: "Who is this one about whom these reports are being related?" Then it is said to him: "Muhammadun rasulu Allah," i.e., "He is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah." This is from the care and attention given to mentioning his virtues ﷺ.

So the sentence whose subject is omitted is considered a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani).

There are other aspects in it, which are not hidden, and the best of them is this.

In this there is a proclamation nullifying the denial of the polytheists of his messengership, when "they refused to have written in the document of the truce: 'This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, agreed upon,' and they said: 'Had we known that you are the Messenger of Allah, we would not have barred you from the House.'"

His saying "wa-alladhina ma'ahu" may be a subject (mubtada'), with "ashiddau" as its predicate, and what follows is information about it, the intent being praise of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The meaning of "ma'ahu" is complete companionship in obedience and support, like His saying, exalted is He: "And Allah said: Indeed I am with you." The intent is all of his Companions, not specifically the people of al-Hudaybiyah.

And even if they were the primary intended group, they were known for the truthfulness of what they pledged to Allah. For this reason, "when the Muslims were routed on the day of Hunayn, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib: 'Call out, O people of the acacia tree (usul al-samurah)!'"

It is also permissible that "wa-alladhina ma'ahu" be a conjunction (atf) upon "rasulihi" from His saying: "He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth." The estimated form is: "and He sent those who are with him," i.e., his Companions, with "sending" understood to include permission given to them through the mediation of the Messenger ﷺ, like His saying, exalted is He: "When We sent to them two" (Ya-Sin: 14), the verse, for the messengers to the people of Antioch were among the disciples, whom Jesus had commanded to spread guidance and monotheism. So the sending is the dispatching of him in His saying, exalted is He: "We sent against you servants of Ours" (al-Isra': 5). On this basis, "arsalna" in this verse is used in both its literal and its figurative sense.

"Ashiddau" is the plural of "shadid," which is the one described with intense firmness in the immaterial sense, namely severity and harshness in dealing. Allah, exalted is He, said describing the Fire: "Over it are angels, stern and severe" (al-Tahrim: 6).

Firmness against the disbelievers is firmness in fighting them and showing enmity towards them. This is a description of praise, because the believers who were with the Prophet ﷺ were the party of truth and the spreaders of Islam, so nothing befits them except displaying anger for Allah, love for Allah, and hatred for Allah's sake, which is part of faith. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ were the strongest of believers in faith, due to the radiance of prophetic light upon their hearts; therefore it is inevitable that they would be firmer against the disbelievers, for between the souls of the two groups there is complete opposition. Their dislike of the truce with the disbelievers on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, and their eagerness to kill the captives whom they had seized that day, which the Prophet ﷺ pardoned, were nothing but effects of their firmness against the disbelievers, and the superior interest in fighting and killing, which the Prophet ﷺ preferred, had not yet become apparent to them.

For this reason, the one who argued most in refusing the truce that day, being the firmest of them against the disbelievers, was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, while the one most understanding of the interest which the Prophet ﷺ sought in concluding the truce was Abu Bakr. Sahl ibn Hunayf said on the day of Siffin: "O people, suspect opinion, for we saw ourselves on the day of Abu Jandal, and had we been able to refuse the Messenger of Allah's action, we would have refused it, and Allah and His Messenger know best."

Then the rulings of firmness against the disbelievers, from obligation, recommendation, and permissibility, and the rulings of keeping their company and dealing with them, proceed according to the various circumstances, and the scholars of Islam have discussions on them. Much of that has already been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran and in Surat Bara'ah.

The firmness against the disbelievers they took from the firmness of the Prophet ﷺ in establishing the religion. Allah said: "Towards the believers he is kind and merciful" (al-Tawbah: 128).

As for their being merciful among themselves, that is due to the firmness of the brotherhood of faith among them in their souls.

"Like a seed-crop" is its predicate, which is the parable. This is the apparent meaning from the context of the verse, so it refers to something like His saying in the Gospel of Matthew (chapter 13, verse 3): "Behold, a sower went forth to sow [meaning Jesus, peace be upon him], and as he sowed, some fell by the way side, and the birds came and devoured it," until he said: "And other fell on good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty." He said in another verse: "Now the sower on good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty."

This includes the growth of faith in their hearts, and that they call people to the religion until the believers increase, just as one grain produces a hundred ears, and just as a great tree grows from a seed.

In His saying "it has brought forth its shoot" (*akhraja shatˀahu*), there is a metaphor: bringing out is applied to the branching off of shoots from the grain, by likening the branching to coming out, and likening the original plant from which it branches to something that brings forth a thing from a place.

The word *shatˀ* (with a hamza at its end and a sukun on the *ṭāʾ*) means the young shoots of the crop and the offshoots of the grain. It is said: *ashṭaʾa al-zarʿ* (the crop put forth shoots), when it sends out branches.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read it with a sukun on the *ṭāʾ* and with a hamza. Ibn Kathir read *shaṭaʾahu*, with a fatha on the *ṭāʾ* followed by an alif, by softening the hamza into an alif.

*Āzarahu* means "strengthened it." It derives from *al-muʾāzara* with a hamza, which is assistance. It is derived from the noun *al-izār* (the waist-wrap), because it binds the back of the one who wears it and its tying helps him in work and carrying, as has been said. But in my view the more evident position is the reverse: that the waist-wrap's name is derived from *āzara*, because deriving verbs from fixed nouns (*jāmid*) is rare, and one does not resort to it unless it is necessary. The *mufāʿala* form in *āzarahu* is used metaphorically to express the strength of the action, like the expressions "may Allah grant you well-being" (*ʿāfākā Allāh*) and His saying, exalted is He, "and blessed therein" (*wa bāraka fīhā*).

The pronoun that is the subject in *āzarahu* refers to the shoot, and the object pronoun refers to the seed-crop; that is, the shoot strengthened its root.

[Page 209]

The majority read *fa-āzarahu*. Ibn Dhakwan, from Ibn ʿAmir, read *fa-azzarahu* without an alif after the hamza, and the meaning is the same.

The meaning of *istaghlaẓa* is that it became very thick in its kind. The *sīn* and the *tāʾ* are for emphasis, like in *istajāba* (he responded).

The two pronouns that are subjects in *istaghlaẓa* and *istawā* refer to the seed-crop.

*Al-sawaq* is the plural of *sāq* (stalk) in an irregular way, because *sāq* is not an adjective; it is a noun on the pattern *faʿal* with two fathas.

All readers read *ʿalā sūqihi* with a *wāw* after the damma. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Ibn Kathir read *sūʾqihi* with a hamza, meaning a silent hamza after the damma of the *sīn*. This is a weak dialect in which they make a hamza of the *wāw* preceded by a damma. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"La-ḥabbu al-muʾqidāni ilayya Mūsā"*

It is attributed to Qunbul from Ibn Kathir, but the exegetes did not mention it, and it is not mentioned in *Ḥirz al-Amānī*. Al-Nawawi mentioned it in the book *Ghayth al-Nafʿ*, but his statement is not clear regarding the correctness of attributing this reading to Qunbul.

The stalk of a crop or a tree is the base from which ears and branches come out.

The meaning of this parable is the comparison of the state of the beginning of the Muslims and their growth until they became many. This includes the comparison of the beginning of the religion of Islam, weak, and its strengthening day by day until its affair became firm and it prevailed over its enemies.

This parable is open to considering the comparison in its parts, such that Muhammad (ﷺ) is compared to the sower, as Jesus gave a parable of the victory of Islam in the Gospel. The believers are compared to the grains of the crop that he sows in the earth, such as Abu Bakr, Khadija, ʿAli, Bilal and ʿAmmar. The shoot is those who supported the Muslims. The Prophet (ﷺ) called to Allah alone, and a small group joined him; then Allah strengthened him with those who supported him, just as the first stalk of the crop is strengthened by what surrounds it of what is produced from it, until it pleases the farmers.

His saying "it pleases the farmers" (*yuʿjibu al-zurrāʿa*) is an embellishment of the thing compared, so as to convey the embellishment of the thing being compared.

* * *

"That He may enrage the disbelievers by them" is a reason for what their parable with the crop, described by their growth and advancement in increase and strength, implies. Because their being in that state is by Allah's decree for them to be in it, He described it as done so that He might enrage the disbelievers by them.

Al-Qurtubi said: Abu ʿUrwa al-Zubayri said: "We were with Malik ibn Anas, and they mentioned to him a man who belittled the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Malik then recited this verse, "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah..." until he reached His saying, "that He may enrage the disbelievers by them." Malik said: 'Whoever among the people has rancor in his heart toward any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), this verse applies to him.'" I said: "May Allah have mercy on Malik ibn Anas and be pleased with him; how subtle is his derivation."

* * *

"Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness and a great reward."

After highlighting their status and praising them, He followed this with the promise of reward for the qualities they possess, which have a firm effect in spreading and supporting this religion.

His saying "among them" (*minhum*) may be that *min* is explanatory, as in His saying: "So avoid the abomination of the idols" (Al-Hajj: 30).

[Page 211]

This is a common usage. It may also be kept in its apparent meaning of partitive, because it is a promise to everyone who is with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the present and the future. The mention of *min* then serves as a warning. This does not contradict forgiveness for all of them, because all of them believed and did righteous deeds, and the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) are the elite of the believers.

The Surah of Al-Fath ends here.

Surah Al-Hujurat

It is named "Surat al-Hujurat" in all the codices (*maṣāhif*), books of Sunnah and tafsir, and it has no other name. The reason for its naming is that the word "al-Hujurat" (the private apartments) is mentioned in it. It was revealed concerning the incident of the Banu Tamim calling out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from behind his apartments, so it became known by this addition.

It is Medinan by the consensus of the people of interpretation (*ahl al-taʾwil*), meaning that it was revealed after the Hijra. Al-Suyuti in *al-Itqan* related an anomalous opinion that it is Meccan, but the one who holds this opinion is not known.

In *Asbab al-Nuzul* of al-Wahidi, His saying, exalted is He, "O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female" (Al-Hujurat: 13), and the rest of the verse, was revealed in Mecca on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, as will come. But it did not establish that this verse was revealed in Mecca, as will come. And in *al-Itqan* he did not count it among the surahs of which some verses are excepted.

It is the one hundred and eighteenth surah in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Mujadila and before Surat al-Tahrim. The revelation of this surah was in the ninth year (AH). Its first verse concerns the delegation of the Banu Tamim, as will come at His saying, exalted is He, "O you who believe, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger" (Al-Hujurat: 1), and His saying, "Indeed, those who call you from behind the apartments, most of them do not understand" (Al-Hujurat: 4).

All those who counted its verses counted them as eighteen verses.

* * *

The purposes of this surah

Its purposes relate to events that happened close to one another, which were the cause of the revelation of the rulings and etiquettes in it.

The first of them is teaching the Muslims some of the manners that are obligatory for them with the Prophet (ﷺ) in

[Page 214]

his dealings, his address, and his calling. What prompted the teaching of them was the rudeness of the Bedouins displayed by the delegation of the Banu Tamim when they called the Messenger (ﷺ) from his houses, as will come at His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, those who call you from behind the apartments, most of them do not understand" (Al-Hujurat: 4).

And the obligation of the Muslims' truthfulness in what they report, and verification in conveying news in general, and that this is a trait of the believers; and avoiding the manners of the disbelievers and the defiantly disobedient (*fasiqin*). It touches on the fighting that happens among the Muslims and reconciling between them because they are brothers; and what Allah commanded of the manners of good dealing among Muslims in their conditions, in private and in public. From this it moves on to warning against remnants of disbelief's character in some rude Bedouins, straightening their crookedness.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said, while explaining His saying, exalted is He: "O you who believe, if a defiant one (*fasiq*) comes to you with news, verify it" (Al-Hujurat: 6): This surah contains guidance for the believers to noble character. It is either with Allah, or with His Messenger (ﷺ), or with others of the human kind, and they are of two categories: either they are following the path of the believers and within the rank of obedience, or they are outside it, which is defiance (*fusuq*). The one who is within their group is either present with them or absent from them. So these are five divisions. He said: Allah mentioned in this surah five times "O you who believe" (Al-Hujurat: 6), and after each time He guided to a noble trait relating to one of the five divisions. We will come to the rest of his speech when explaining the first verse of this surah.

This surah is the first of the surahs of al-Mufassal, with the *ṣād* doubled, and it is called *al-Muḥkam* according to one opinion in the school (*madhhab*), which is the one preferred by the later jurists. Regarding the starting point of al-Mufassal according to us there are ten opinions, the most famous two: it is said that its beginning is Surat Qaf, and it is said that it is Surat al-Hujurat. Regarding the starting point of the middle of al-Mufassal, there are two opinions, the more correct being that it is Surat ʿAbasa. Regarding its short surahs, there are two opinions, the more correct being that it begins with Surat al-Duha.

The Hanafis differed about the starting point of al-Mufassal, with twelve opinions, and the preferred one is that its beginning is from

al-Hujurat, and the beginning of the middle of al-Mufassal is Surat al-Tariq, and the beginning of the short surahs is Surat Idha Zulzilat al-Ard.

According to the Shafiis, it is said that the beginning of al-Mufassal is Surat al-Hujurat, and it is said Surat Qaf. Ibn Kathir preferred it in his tafsir, as will come.

According to the Hanbalis: the beginning of al-Mufassal is Surat Qaf.

Al-Mufassal (the "detailed" portion of the Qur'an) is the surahs with which it is recommended to recite some of them in some of the five daily prayers, as is explained in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*).
